detail.abstract: This study details the development of BloodGo, a mobile application designed to improve the blood donation process in Malaysia. The application aims to provide a centralized platform connecting blood donors, recipients, and blood banks to manage and coordinate donations more efficiently. BloodGo was developed to address common issues such as low donor turnout, a lack of real-time information on blood availability, and poor communication between donors and healthcare facilities. Key features of the app include donor registration, real-time blood inventory updates, emergency alerts, donation scheduling, and personalized notifications, all of which simplify the donation process and encourage regular participation. The development followed an Agile prototyping model, which allowed for continuous user feedback and step-by-step improvements. Testing results indicate that BloodGo enhances donor engagement, assists hospitals in managing blood supply more effectively, and improves coordination during emergencies. The project demonstrates the potential of mobile technology to create a more efficient, accessible, and reliable blood donation system to support the healthcare sector.

detail.title: Digital Government in Brazil and the AI Plan: Opportunities, Risks and a 2028 Agenda
detail.abstract: This article examines Brazil's trajectory in building digital government and implementing the Brazilian Strategy for Artificial Intelligence (EBIA), emphasizing three fronts: digital public services (gov.br), instant payments (Pix) and the central bank digital currency (Drex). Combining empirical evidence drawn from daily use of services and international experiences (Estonia, Dubai, Colombia and New York), academic literature and official documents, it discusses gains in efficiency and inclusion and the countervailing risks arising from data centralization, algorithmic opacity and threats to privacy. The paper synthesizes evidence on adoption, benefits, concerns and safeguards for each digital public infrastructure and formulates three hypotheses relating efficiency, inclusion and trust. Building on comparative experiences, it proposes an agenda up to 2028 grounded in independent algorithm audits, privacy by design, proportionality and regulatory independence, as well as digital literacy and ethical governance. The goal is to contribute to international debates on digital governance from a Latin American perspective while outlining conditions under which centralized infrastructures can serve both state efficiency and citizen rights.

detail.title: How Livestreaming E-commerce Reshapes Consumers' Product Return Behaviors: A Tri-processing Theory Perspective
detail.abstract: Livestreaming e-commerce (LEC) is transforming online shopping by enhancing consumer experiences and boosting sales. However, should retailers adopt LEC solely based on its potential for sales growth? This study examines the impact of introducing LEC on consumer purchases and product returns by comparing it to traditional e-commerce (TEC). Extending the tri-processing theory to the LEC context and integrating it with the LEC and channel introduction literature, we examine the impact of LEC exposure beyond consumers' purchasing to product returns behaviors. We leverage a novel dataset from a leading retailer in China that adopted LEC in July 2017. Employing difference-indifferences (DID), regression discontinuity in time (RDiT), and instrumental variable (IV) estimation approaches, our findings reveal that LEC increases sales by 95% in value and 111% in quantity. However, it also results in an 86% increase in the value of returns and a 50% increase in return frequency. Notably, most returns occur at the pre-shipping stage. We further identify consumers' self-control failure as a critical moderator of tri-processing theory, indicating that consumers lacking self-control are less likely to correct their purchase decisions early. Furthermore, we find that increased product returns at the pre-shipping stage are associated with more negative emotions compared to returns in the post-shipping stage. Finally, we analyze how LEC disrupts retailers' cost structures related to each return stage. Our research contributes to tri-processing theory by applying it to a multi-stage decision-making context in online shopping and highlighting self-control as an important moderator for activating Type 3 processing. Our work provides valuable guidelines for retailers and platforms considering the adoption of LEC.

affiliations: American Enterprise Institute

detail.title: A Law Enforcement Paradigm for the New Form of Money

publicationDetails.detailsText: Case Western Reserve University Journal of Law Technology and the Internet (Spring 2026)

detail.abstract: Over the last two centuries, transfers of money have evolved from movements of tangible things to digital communications events. Over the last half-century, financial surveillance law has taken root. The product of the two trends is a comprehensive, global financial surveillance regime that has substantial costs in both dollar terms and in values, such as privacy, free speech, and autonomy. Those costs appear to vastly outstrip the benefits of such surveillance. Along with its infirmity as policy, general financial surveillance stands on shaky constitutional ground in the United States. It impedes the full development of digital forms of money and the benefits they offer. Privacy "tiering" in digital money and cryptocurrency cannot correct the imbalance. To replace broad financial surveillance, this article proposes a new paradigm for the new form of money, a system through which law enforcement agencies could query digital transactors for investigative purposes. In a communications channel parallel to private transaction channels, law enforcement requests could be transmitted selectively from anywhere on the globe to transactors anywhere else, inviting them to help suppress and punish criminal activity. Such a system would maintain or strengthen law enforcement capabilities while obviating the existing, broad and costly financial surveillance regime. Through a discussion of the system's social and criminological dimensions, this article reveals and outlines its technical sides. Questions include the effect of such a system on secrecy in law enforcement investigations, and the prospect of legally mandating responses to law enforcement queries. Because a system for communicating law enforcement queries to global transactors would be "retail," it would allow for political feedback loops that cause law enforcement practices and priorities to hew more closely to public values than the current "wholesale" financial surveillance system. Digital money and cryptocurrency transaction models could be tuned to more acutely protect privacy while maintaining a channel for communication with law enforcement.

title: Persuasion and Leverage: Free Trial and Menu Design in Software Purchase

detail.title: Persuasion and Leverage: Free Trial and Menu Design in Software Purchase
detail.abstract: Problem definition: Offering a free trial before integrating software modules has been widely adopted by IT vendors to mitigate bilateral uncertainty about IT performance. This paper examines a sequential mechanism of free trial and contract menu for software purchase, dealing with both uncertain information and private information. We also classify the degree of software complexity by information growth rate of free trial learning. Methodology/results: In the persuasion-contract model, we depict boundaries where signal structures satisfy the condition, and an optimal trial duration enables IT vendor to update both parties’ beliefs on performance, regarded as persuasion effect. When the client has private efficiency (type), we find information rent increase in the duration, defined as information leverage effect. This yields a pivot finding that shrinking the uncertainty on performance amplifies the value of private efficiency. With low probability of high type, free trial is less likely to be offered or shorter mainly due to information leverage effect. With the high probability, IT vendor is more likely to adopt free trial with longer duration, achieving almost unencumbered persuasion effect. Intriguingly, the duration increases but information rent decreases with software complexity. Managerial implications: Grounded in onion architecture of software design, we derive the complete design on trial duration and customized menu. When the probability of high performance is moderate and performance differentiation is high, free trial has the persuasion power. In the menu, software prices for both types increases with the duration. The optimal duration first increases then decreases with probability of high performance, and always increases with probability of high type. As software increases the complexity, the vendor extends the trial and implements steeper price increments for high type.

title: Generative AI in Legal Education: A Two-Year Experiment with ChatGPT
affiliations: Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam

detail.title: Generative AI in Legal Education: A Two-Year Experiment with ChatGPT
detail.abstract:
This report hopes to contribute to the discussion around the use of generative AI in legal education.
The literature is currently divided: some celebrate ChatGPT’s potential to assist drafting and reasoning; others warn of shortcut learning and degraded skill acquisition. I seek to add evidence to this scholarly debate in two ways. First, I review the growing body of studies reporting experiments conducted in law schools, with the aim of offering readers a repository of pedagogical initiatives that they can replicate and refine in their own classroom.

Second, I present findings from a two-year experiment of my own, in which students faced different teaching techniques around generative AI: prohibition, unstructured exposure, and structured training. I find that structured training produced a clear advantage in the first year, but its edge diminished as baseline familiarity with AI spread in the second. The experiment also suggests that failing to teach students how to use AI effectively and responsibly is a missed opportunity, yet its absence does not lead to the systemic breakdown that some have forecast.

I draw practical lessons from these observations. In the short term, law school boards should resist the temptation to impose one-size-fits-all choices on the entire faculty body. Instead, professors should retain freedom to experiment. In the medium term, I suggest that (current) long-form writing (such as master theses) should be retired. Finally, law schools will benefit from investing in AI literacy for both students and professors if they want to remain attractive in the long run.

detail.abstract: Civil engineering has historically been the backbone of human civilization, from the irrigation canals of Mesopotamia to the smart cities of the 21st century. While technology-driven fields such as computer science have experienced cycles of boom and saturation, civil engineering remains indispensable because it addresses fundamental physical needs that cannot be outsourced or automated. This paper analyzes why civil engineering is positioned to become the defining career of the 2030s. Drawing on global investment forecasts, it highlights the $94 trillion infrastructure gap projected by 2040, the accelerating demands of urbanization, climate resilience, and post-conflict reconstruction. Case studies from India, the United States, China, and Africa illustrate how mega-infrastructure programs are reshaping labor markets and career opportunities. The paper also explores the role of emerging technologies such as Artificial Intelligence, Building Information Modeling (BIM), digital twins, robotics, and sustainable materials, showing how these tools will transform the profession. Finally, it considers challenges such as regulatory hurdles, environmental compliance, and the need for cross-disciplinary skills. The findings suggest that civil engineering will not only remain a resilient profession but will evolve into a global driver of economic growth, sustainability, and innovation in the coming decades.

detail.title: Infrastructure Capacity, Risk, and Firm Value: Evidence from U.S. Electricity Tightness

publicationDetails.detailsText: HKU Jockey Club Enterprise Sustainability Global Research Institute Paper No. 2025/136
publicationDetails.journalName: Hong Kong University Business School: HKU Jockey Club Enterprise Sustainability Global Research Institute Paper Series

detail.abstract: Real-time bottlenecks in non-storable infrastructure-most visibly electricity-can throttle modern production, yet standard models treat capacity as unlimited. We embed proportional rationing of grid supply into multi-sector economy, showing that unexpected scarcity cuts output, employment, and consumption, while the prospect of future capacity expansions mitigates those losses. To test the model's predictions, we measure U.S. public firms' exposure to realized electric capacity constraints and future expected capacity tightness. We confirm the model's predictions using panel regressions with fixed effects and establish causality by exploiting two quasi-natural experiments: the 2021 Texas blackout (a 34 GW supply shock) and subsequent state reforms that raised future expected capacity. Difference-in-differences estimates indicate a drop in short-term profitability and firm value in affected firms. Higher future anticipated capacity leads to higher longer-term employment, capital, and firm value. Investors demand higher expected returns for firms with greater exposure to electric capacity constraints, confirming that infrastructure tightness, either due to excess demand or limited supply, is a priced, macro-critical risk.

detail.abstract: Organizational behavior has long been studied through classical frameworks of psychology and psychometrics, where constructs such as decision-making competence, job satisfaction, and agreement are measured as independent or linearly related variables. Yet organizational life frequently displays paradoxes: leaders with high decision-making competence yet low job satisfaction, staff with strong agreement but divergent performance, or simultaneous alignment and misalignment across different groups. Such non-classical dynamics resist conventional models. This monograph introduces Organizational Quantum Psychometric Modelling (OQPM), a quantum-inspired paradigm that rethinks the measurement and interpretation of organizational behavior. Drawing on principles of quantum theory—particularly entanglement, superposition, and synchronization—OQPM proposes that leader–staff relationships can be modeled as coupled systems where states of competence, satisfaction, and agreement are not merely correlated but interdependent in ways that defy classical logic. OQPM advances the idea that organizational measures exist in “superposed” states until relational contexts collapse them into observable outcomes, and that entangled states explain paradoxical findings where one group’s strengths are systematically paired with the other’s deficits. By reframing psychometric constructs through a quantum lens, OQPM seeks to provide a more nuanced framework for capturing variability, paradox, and interdependence in organizational life. This paradigm opens avenues for new metrics, predictive models, and empirical inquiries that could enrich both organizational psychology and leadership studies, while laying the foundation for the emerging field of Organizational Quantum Psychology.

title: Transitional Fairness and Recognition of Prior Learning under the SQE: A Public Law and Comparative Analysis
affiliations: Independent Legal Researcher

detail.title: Transitional Fairness and Recognition of Prior Learning under the SQE: A Public Law and Comparative Analysis
detail.abstract:
This paper offers a doctrinal and policy analysis of the Solicitors Qualifying Examination (SQE) within the statutory framework of the Legal Services Act 2007 (LSA 2007). It argues that the SQE’s uniform assessment regime—requiring all candidates, including those with accredited Level 7 legal qualifications, to undertake full retesting—creates disproportionate exclusionary effects that cannot be justified under principles of proportionality or the Public Sector Equality Duty (PSED).1 Through detailed engagement with case law, regulatory policy, and comparative jurisdictions, the paper demonstrates that high and inflexible SQE costs function as regulatory harms in themselves, entrenching socio-economic disadvantage and constraining diversity within the profession.2 Evidence from Canada, Ireland, and Australia shows that Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) can provide a proportionate mechanism for competence assurance, using equivalence mapping and external moderation to reduce duplication and lower financial barriers.3 The argument develops in three stages. Section 6 examines the SQE’s cost burdens as structural harms, applying proportionality doctrine (Bank Mellat v HM Treasury (No 2)) and equality principles to show how financial architecture embeds exclusion.4 Section 6.4 links these findings to access to justice, demonstrating how exclusion from the profession narrows consumer choice, undermines competition, and weakens the representative legitimacy of solicitors.5 Section 7 proposes a safeguarded domestic RPL pathway, showing its compatibility with international precedent and with the SRA’s statutory duties under the LSA 2007. 

The conclusion is that the SQE, in its current form, risks failing the proportionality standard confirmed in R (Lumsdon) v Legal Services Board and contravenes the regulatory objectives of the LSA 2007.6 A restructured RPL pathway would deliver a legally defensible, economically efficient, and socially equitable reform, aligning competence assurance with statutory commitments to diversity, access, and the consumer interest.

detail.title: The Apathy Economy: Patents, Advertising, and Consumer Indifference

publicationDetails.journalName: University of Arizona James E. Rogers College of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Patents function as signals as well as rights to exclude. They inform competitors, investors, employees, and consumers about the invention and its owner. How this information affects consumers is not well understood. Existing studies disagree about how advertising a product or service as patented, or patent pending, affects the price consumers will pay. This Article offers the first major empirical study of that question and finds that consumers behave with surprising rationality: they will not pay any price premium for a patented product. A product’s patent status conveys little information about whether it is superior to competing offerings. The results hold across different products and consumer characteristics.

These findings have critical implications for both patent and advertising law. They suggest the changes to patent marking rules in the American Invents Act were irrelevant. They also indicate that the theoretical problems with patent advertising do not substantially exist in practice, making systemic reforms unjustified. Similarly, falsely advertising something as patented should not create liability under federal trademark law because such claims are irrelevant to consumer purchasing decisions. Finally, the inclusion of patent status in consumer advertising is a puzzle. The Article hypothesizes that such advertising occurs due to mixed audiences for content, efforts to bolster brands, and competition for employees.

title: Climate Risk Exposure and Firms' Climate Strategies
affiliations: London Business School and Columbia University

detail.title: Climate Risk Exposure and Firms' Climate Strategies
detail.abstract: When exposed to greater physical and transition climate risks, are firms more likely to engage in climate mitigation, climate adaptation, or/and political strategies? This study examines this question and finds that firms exposed to greater physical and transition climate risks are less likely to undertake substantial mitigation efforts. Instead, they pursue other strategies. Specifically, firms exposed to greater physical climate risks are more inclined to pursue adaptation strategies, while firms facing higher transition climate risks are more likely to engage in anti-climate political strategies (such as lobbying against climate policies). The intensity of how firms manage their climate risks is influenced by their time horizon: the more myopic they are, the less they engage in climate mitigation and the more they oppose climate-friendly policies, thereby decreasing transition risks today while worsening their exposure to future physical and transition climate risks. Overall, this study provides insights into the (lack of) preparedness of the corporate sector for heightened climate risks.

detail.abstract: In the highly connected digital world of today, cybersecurity has presented itself as a primary risk factor for any business and not merely an IT concern. This article addresses how Program Managers can act as a focal point in raising cybersecurity awareness among teams, ensuring that security features do not become an afterthought but are incorporated into project planning and execution from the onset. Throughout the lifecycle of projects, Program Managers create a security-oriented culture by aligning various cross-functional teams, integrating cybersecurity requirements, and setting up security gates. As a result, Program Managers act as organizational risk partners, integrating risk and compliance requirements as well as communication strategies. From preserving continuity of operations to attaining sustainable business resilience, Program Manager engagement in cybersecurity remains vital with ever-increasing threats that are more complex and greater in volume.

title: Bridging the Human-AI Alignment Gap: Frameworks for Digital Transformation, Governance, and ROI

detail.title: Bridging the Human-AI Alignment Gap: Frameworks for Digital Transformation, Governance, and ROI
detail.abstract: Despite rapid advances in artificial intelligence capabilities, 70% of enterprise digital transformations continue to fail—less from technical limitations than from what we term the Alignment Gap: the divergence between AI deployment and organizational readiness [2]. This paper proposes human–AI alignment as a critical but overlooked success factor in digital transformation and introduces three novel frameworks addressing this gap. The Strategic Human–AI Alignment Framework (SHAAF) provides enterprise-level architecture, the Human–AI Alignment Score (HAAS™) offers a diagnostic metric for measuring organizational readiness, and the ACT+M™ Readiness Index formalizes leadership and cultural preparedness across five dimensions. We also identify two recurring risk archetypes—Execution Theater and the Misalignment Spiral—that illustrate how misalignment compounds over time. Together, these contributions represent the first systemic attempt to define enterprise-scale diagnostic constructs for human–AI alignment, extending digital transformation and organizational change theory while providing practical tools for practitioners and policy frameworks for governance. They are presented as practitioner-oriented proposals intended to inform governance debates and guide future empirical research.

detail.abstract: The term innovation arbitrage-popularized in technology policy to describe innovators relocating to more permissive jurisdictions (Thierer, 2016)-is here extended into the climate and clean energy domain through the introduction of resilience arbitrage. This framing was first introduced in Daviy (2025) at the Sustainable Energy Forum (SEF), Kyiv. I define resilience arbitrage as the strategic deployment of frontier technologies and startups into sandboxes of resilience-high-need, high-opportunity environments-where acute disruption, urgent demand, and supportive policy create conditions for accelerated piloting, scaling, and refinement.Unlike regulatory sandboxes-temporary policy carve-outs created by regulators-sandboxes of resilience emerge organically in fragile or crisis-affected contexts as real-world testbeds of adaptive capacity, where resilience arbitrage leverages asymmetries in adaptive capacity to transform crisis, constraint, or structural underdevelopment into platforms for accelerated innovation. This framing extends earlier theories of strategic opportunity under incomplete markets (Denrell et al., 2003) and complements the literature on leapfrogging in energy and infrastructure transitions (Zanello et al., 2016; Zaman, 2020). Case evidence from frontier markets underscores this potential. Solar microgrids have provided life-saving energy in Ukrainian hospitals and communities during wartime grid collapse, when diesel generators failed (SolarPower Europe, 2023; Microgrid Knowledge, 2023; Booth et al., 2019). Hybrid renewable systems combining solar, wind, and storage have been validated as technically robust and adaptable in extreme operating conditions (Xu et al., 2019; Adewole et al., 2023). Insights from knowledge arbitrage research (Nawaz et al., 2024) suggest further pathways by which startups can translate fragility into adaptive capacity. Case evidence suggests that piloting in frontier environments not only lowers cost and time-to-market but also expands systemic resilience. This paper contributes to the literatures on innovation arbitrage, technological leapfrogging, and resilience by introducing a framework for resilience arbitrage that integrates site identification, regulatory experimentation, capital mobilization, and cross-sector partnerships. By naming and theorizing this mechanism, it establishes both a conceptual foundation for scholarly debate and a practical strategy for accelerating climate technology deployment in fragile and high-need geographies.

detail.abstract: The growing influence of the Western media in Pakistan poses serious questions concerning the role of youth identity transformation: Is the introduction of global cultural flows to the Pakistani youth part of the cultural convergence or cultural destruction? This is a qualitative work where the use of interpretative phenomenological analysis (IPA) is utilized by examining how the Pakistani young adults iron out the role of Western media in shaping their identity, their way of life as well as their social constructs. These aspects of acculturation are subtle and rarely captured in popular press coverage; using semistructured interviewing with 20 respondents in urban and semi-urban communities in the greater New Orleans area, there are particular nuances of acculturation that include selective use of Western practices and strengthening of local traditions. Results highlight the emergence of hybrid identities that are formed through cultural homogenization, resistance, and glocalization at the same time. By placing the Pakistani youth in a larger discourse of globalization, hybridity and postcolonial identity, this study focuses on youth agency in cultural negotiation. Relevance demonstrates the significance of media literacy programs with culturally based appeal, curriculum revision, and policy advocacy.

detail.abstract: This research examines the systematic pattern of United States-led coups d'état and regime change operations from 1893 to 2011, analyzing their methods, motivations, and long-term consequences. Through qualitative analysis of declassified documents, scholarly sources, and historical records, this study identifies 47 documented instances of American intervention in foreign governments, ranging from early territorial acquisitions like Hawaii to modern military interventions in Libya. The research reveals consistent patterns in American covert operations: economic motivations disguised as ideological concerns, standardised CIA methodologies, and predominantly negative long-term outcomes for targeted nations. Findings indicate that while short-term strategic objectives were occasionally achieved, the majority of interventions resulted in regional instability, anti-American sentiment, and failed democratic transitions. This comprehensive analysis contributes to understanding the effectiveness and ethical implications of American foreign policy tools in the post-World War II era.

detail.abstract: Conventional academic and media accounts depict global stock exchange competition as a contest of regulatory standards to win initial public offerings (IPOs). This Article re-examines global stock exchange competition through a much broader political economy lens. We make two central arguments. First, competition for IPOs, while highly visible, is subject to important qualifications: IPOs provide only marginal revenues for modern exchanges, most firms are unable to engage in regulatory arbitrage to obtain a high-profile foreign listing, and the public markets are increasingly eclipsed by private capital as a rival source of finance. Second, while the role of nation states has been largely ignored in the literature on stock exchange competition, they have keen economic, policy and geopolitical interests in their domestic exchanges. By moving beyond the “race to the bottom” framework and a narrow focus on IPOs, we show how stock exchanges have become strategic assets in a new era of global competition, calling for sustained scholarly engagement across law, economics, and international relations.

detail.abstract: This briefing highlights how South Asian women in Scotland experience abuse in ways often unrecognised by mainstream services. Abuse extends beyond husbands’ violence to include coercion by affinal kin, with forced domestic labour, financial exploitation, sexual coercion, and isolation central to many accounts. Women frequently lacked the language to name these experiences as abuse, leading to delayed recognition and support. Cultural practices and family dynamics meant participants often felt unseen within Scottish policy and service definitions of domestic abuse. Recognising the breadth of these experiences—particularly forced labour and affinal abuse—is vital to ensuring that South Asian women’s realities are accurately reflected in services and public awareness campaigns.

detail.abstract: Maternity waiting homes (MWHs) are increasingly used to increase skilled birth attendance in regions with scarce obstetric services. We seek to optimize their assignment policy, that is whether and when a pregnant woman should go to her local MWH given available accommodation capacity and individual characteristics including living location. Our model leverages clinical data on labor onset and latent phase duration to minimize the predicted number of unassisted deliveries resulting from such policy in the local population. We present explicit mathematical solutions for different variants of this problem and integer program formulations of discretized approximations capturing practical implementation constraints. Our numerical experiments leverage detailed primary and secondary data on the population and health facilities of Bong County, Liberia. They suggest that our proposed pooling and assignment policy interventions for the existing MWH capacity in that region may plausibly halve the incidence rate of unassisted deliveries and reduce the probability of unassisted deliveries for the most vulnerable women from 70% to 15%. Implementing data-driven individual assessments of unassisted delivery risk and MWH assignment policies may thus constitute impactful and low-cost interventions in regions with limited MWH accommodation capacity.

title: Is a Standard Definition of Corporate Social Responsibility Necessary for Its Legal Enforcement in Tanzania?

detail.title: Is a Standard Definition of Corporate Social Responsibility Necessary for Its Legal Enforcement in Tanzania?
detail.abstract: Despite growing awareness of corporate social responsibility (CSR), there is no consensus on its definition. This paper investigates whether a standardised definition of CSR is necessary for its legal enforcement in Tanzania. The paper employed doctrinal legal research to examine the CSR legal framework and identify challenges that a standardised definition of CSR can resolve. The findings highlight that while the meaning of CSR is not in dispute, the definition of CSR remains a subject of debate, ultimately contributing to poor CSR practices in Tanzania. Moreover, the existing CSR legal framework in Tanzania has significant challenges, and having a standardised definition is a key step towards addressing them. Although the paper finds that a standardised definition of CSR is not a complete panacea for challenges in performing CSR obligations, it does contribute to implementing CSR goals.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines the accountability gaps created by the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into corporate decision-making. Traditional doctrines of corporate governance fiduciary duties, foreseeability, and liability attribution presume human intentionality and control. AI systems, particularly those employing machine learning, disrupt these assumptions by introducing opaque, autonomous, and adaptive decision-making processes that challenge existing accountability frameworks.

Drawing on case studies from India, the UK, the EU, and the US, this paper argues that the diffusion of responsibility in AI-driven governance undermines both legal liability and corporate ethics. The central claim advanced here is that limited and functionally defined legal personhood for AI systems analogous to corporate personhood offers a pragmatic solution to restore accountability. By recognizing advanced AI systems as artificial legal persons under regulated conditions, the law can establish a locus of responsibility, facilitate regulatory oversight, and ensure enforceable obligations.

This preprint is based on my LLM dissertation (Jindal Global Law School, 2025). It will be revised into multiple journal articles for submission to international law and technology journals.

title: Revealing Domestic Abuse Realities and Viable Helpseeking Pathways for South Asian Women in Scotland Research Briefing 4 Cultural and Community Dynamics

detail.abstract: Despite evidence of severe, culturally specific patterns of abuse and persistent barriers to support, little research has focused on the experiences of South Asian women in Scotland or how they understand and seek help for domestic abuse. Diversifying Justice addressed this gap through arts-based focus groups (n=15) and narrative interviews (n=14), conducted in Urdu and English, using a feminist, participatory methodology designed to prioritise care, reciprocity, and safe sharing of experiences. This briefing focuses on cultural and community dynamics. Participants described how expectations of marriage “at all costs,” gossip, and fear of judgement kept women silent and in unsafe relationships. Divorce was heavily stigmatised, while cultural and religious teachings were frequently blurred or misused to justify abuse. Limited access to Islamic education left women unaware of their rights. Findings highlight the need to challenge harmful cultural narratives, address stigma, and ensure access to accurate religious and legal knowledge.

title: Sankofa-CIL Framework: Indigenous Continuous Improvement Paradigms in Africa

detail.abstract: Continuous improvement (CI) scholarship has long been dominated by Japanese and Western paradigms such as Kaizen, Lean, and Six Sigma, which prioritize efficiency and standardization. While globally influential, these models often marginalize indigenous African philosophies and fail to resonate with local cultural realities. This concept paper introduces the Sankofa-Continuous Improvement Leadership (Sankofa-CIL) Framework as a decolonial alternative that reclaims Africa's epistemic agency. Anchored in the Akan principle of Sankofa-retrieving ancestral wisdom to inform present and future practice-the framework is reinforced by four foundational value-pillars: Ubuntu (humanity and interconnectedness, Southern Africa), Harambee (collective effort, East Africa), Ubora (excellence, Great Lakes/Swahili region), and Umoja (unity, West Africa/Pan-African thought). Together, these pillars reconceptualize CI as a communal, intergenerational, and culturally embedded practice. The paper combines insights from practice theory, indigenous knowledge systems, and decolonial scholarship to position Sankofa-CIL as both restorative-reclaiming marginalized philosophies-and innovative, offering a culturally grounded alternative to imported models of improvement. While this paper focuses on four pillars to establish conceptual clarity, future research will extend the framework to incorporate Central and North African traditions, ensuring a truly pan-African perspective. This phased approach allows for early scholarly dialogue while leaving space for empirical validation and theoretical refinement in subsequent studies.

title: Search without Recall and Gaussian Learning: Structural Properties and Optimal Policies
affiliations: University of Virginia - Darden School of Business, University of Virginia - Darden School of Business and University of Virginia - Darden School of Business

detail.title: Search without Recall and Gaussian Learning: Structural Properties and Optimal Policies
detail.abstract: We tackle the longstanding open problem of optimal stopping in sequential search with no recall under unknown Gaussian parameters. Our analysis disproves Rothschild (1974)'s conjecture that the Reservation Price Property universally holds for search with no recall under Bayesian learning with a conjugate prior. In the early stage of search, a patient decision maker having a sufficiently ample sampling horizon should continue search after a obtaining an arbitrarily high offer. In fact, continuing search regardless of the value of the offer may be optimal if the search cost is sufficiently low. Past a critical sample size, however, a standard single-threshold rule becomes optimal. We explore the factors influencing the critical sample size, and show how to efficiently compute the optimal policy.

title: History Reset and Reputation Effects
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: History Reset and Reputation Effects
detail.abstract: This study analyzes a repeated game between a patient, long-lived player (e.g., a firm) and a sequence of short-lived players (e.g., consumers). A patient player is either an honest type, who mechanically takes a commitment action without resetting history, or an opportunistic type, who strategically chooses actions and resets history at no cost. This study develops a theoretical model of reputation formation and establishes an explicit lower bound for the equilibrium payoff of an opportunistic-type firm in any Nash equilibrium and proves that this bound converges to the Stackelberg payoff as the discount factor approaches 1, given sufficient space richness. Furthermore, it analyzes reputation dynamics in a product choice game with perfect monitoring. It demonstrates that the opportunistic-type firm maintains the incentive to mimic the commitment action until accumulating a sufficiently long history of good records.

title: Will Cooperating with More Influencers Improve Livestream Resilience? Roles of Hybrid Channel and Negative Externality in Influencer Risk Management
affiliations: School of Business Administration, South China University of Technology, South China University of Technology - School of Business Administration (SBA), University of Nottingham, Ningbo - University of Nottingham Ningbo China and University of Southampton, Southampton Business School, Department of Decision Analytics and Risk

detail.title: Will Cooperating with More Influencers Improve Livestream Resilience? Roles of Hybrid Channel and Negative Externality in Influencer Risk Management
detail.abstract: Livestream e-commerce has enabled influencers to play an increasingly critical role in driving consumer engagement. But once livestream accidents occur, a significant negative network externality will be triggered that damages consumer trust and channel performance.  This paper examines how brands can manage such risks by structuring their influencer collaborations through one or more influencer participation. We develop a hybrid channel co-opetition model that accounts for livestream accident risks and endogenous demand shifts among multiple channels. We reveal that, for the brand, cooperating with more influencers helps generate efficiency gains from reduced double marginalization, broader demand expansion, and a competition-mitigating effect, but also induces more significant livestream competition and sharper profit loss when the negative network effect is intensified.  By contrast, influencers as a group typically benefit from more demand through greater reach and redundancy, yet the additional sales do not always translate into a higher profit, as internal influencer competition compresses profit margins and increases the channel coordination cost.  Beyond brand profit, we analyze consumer surplus, which rises with higher commission rates but declines with stronger negative network effects, with the decline more pronounced in the dual-influencer case. To evaluate resilience, we propose a risk-loss index that measures the relative reduction of brand profit under accidents.  We find that the dual-influencer strategy enhances resilience when market expansion is modest or when negative network effects are weak, but this advantage vanishes once the externality intensifies. Overall, our findings highlight how influencer collaborations simultaneously shape consumer surplus and resilience, underscoring the need for brands and platforms to balance demand expansion with effective risk management.

detail.abstract: Even though sustainable public procurement is critical to achieving global climate goals, most public organizations struggle to implement it. While artificial intelligence holds promise for addressing these challenges, its use in the public sector remains limited and often confined to discrete stages of the procurement lifecycle. This paper critically examines artificial intelligence's potential to support sustainable public procurement across the full procurement lifecycle-from defining needs and assessing markets to issuing tenders, evaluating suppliers, and refining practices. Further, we examine the limitations and challenges posed by artificial intelligence technology for public procurement managers, recognizing concerns related to transparency, fairness, governance, and the impacts of artificial intelligencedriven decisions on market competition. Drawing on numerous examples in the practice, our findings show that artificial intelligence can be a powerful bridge between high-level sustainability aspirations and practical implementation, offering procurement officials the ability to access, interpret, and apply vast amounts of sustainability information across the entire procurement lifecycle. Our results provide understanding necessary to leverage artificial intelligence toward advancing sustainability across the entire procurement lifecycle, while highlighting the need for transparent, data-rich systems and collaborative engagement among technical experts, procurement professionals, and compliance and sustainability specialists. This analysis offers actionable insights into how AI can transform sustainable public procurement from aspiration to operational reality, enabling the public sector to use its considerable purchasing power to contribute meaningfully to global climate action.

title: What drives Information Asymmetry? Vagueness Disclosure and Buyside Information Hoarding
affiliations: and Shenzhen University - Shenzhen Audencia Business School

detail.title: What drives Information Asymmetry? Vagueness Disclosure and Buyside Information Hoarding
detail.abstract: This paper examines how the conflicting incentives of different investors during corporate site visits affect market information asymmetry. We investigate whether buy-side investors, who profit from trading, engage in information hoarding, in contrast to sell-side analysts, who profit from sharing information. Leveraging a unique Chinese regulation that mandates the disclosure of survey participant lists, we identify the participation of buy-side and sell-side investors and find strong evidence supporting the information hoarding hypothesis. Our core findings are threefold: First, classic measures of information asymmetry rise significantly immediately following buy-side surveys. Second, we find evidence consistent with informed pre-announcement trading by these investors. Consequently, the participation of buy-side investors, but not sellside analysts, leads to a significantly muted market reaction to subsequent earnings surprises. A textual analysis of over 30,000 survey records reveals that firms strategically cooperate in this behavior, using significantly more vague language in their public disclosures when buy-side investors are present. Our results are robust to an instrumental variable approach that addresses endogeneity concerns. We uncover a dark side of private communication: instead of facilitating information dissemination, investor surveys with the buy-side, potentially with the firm's collusion, can be a source of information asymmetry.

detail.abstract: This study employs the Gender and Development (GAD) framework to examine gender-based disparities in Nigeria's agricultural value chains, using evidence from the cassava value chain (CVC) in Oyo and Benue states. It employs a mixed-methods design that combines quantitative data from a survey of 315 participants with qualitative insights from in-depth interviews (IDIs) and focus group discussions (FGDs). Findings reveal significant disparities in education, land ownership, credit access, and income. 39.5% of female-headed households, compared to 14.2% of male-headed households, had no formal education. Land access for women was 19.8%, compared with 49.6% for men, and only 16.1% of women accessed credit, compared with 48.7% of men. Income disparities were similarly wide, with 74% of female-headed households concentrated in the lowest revenue band (₦100,000-₦999,999), compared to 49% of maleheaded households. Regional differences highlight a commercial orientation in Oyo, where 26.1% of farms exceed 10 acres and harvests are sold directly to intermediaries. In Benue, only 7.6% of farms exceed 10 acres, with cassava largely processed for household consumption. Qualitative findings stress how cultural norms, unpaid care work, and restricted mobility confine women to low-paying processing roles and limit decision-making power. To address these disparities, we recommend implementing gender-responsive land reforms, financial inclusion initiatives, targeted skill development programs, literacy and education initiatives, and women-led cooperatives. Mainstreaming gender in budgeting and extension services is also crucial. Such interventions align with Sustainable Development Goals on poverty reduction, zero hunger, gender equality, decent work, and reduced inequalities.

The primary objective is to assess the advantages and disadvantages of these measures for both the U.S. economy and the global economic environment. detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Black Belt OS™ (BB-OS) as a structural discovery rather than a managerial invention. Despite more than a century of contributions from classical and contemporary schools of management-ranging from Taylor, Fayol, and Weber to Porter, Drucker, Mintzberg, Kotler, and frameworks such as Lean, Agile, EOS, and OKRs-no explicit and testable structural law of human organization has been declared. The BB-OS addresses this gap by proposing that every functional human collective, from families and tribes to corporations, empires, and prospective interplanetary colonies, inevitably operates through nine essential, universal, irreducible processes. These processes are independent of tools, platforms, or technologies, and their absence leads to structural failure. The paper contributes in three dimensions: (i) structural proposition, by articulating the BB-OS as a universal organizational law; (ii) scientific framing, by establishing clear criteria of falsifiability and reproducibility; and (iii) cross-scale applicability, by demonstrating its validity across biological, social, and civilizational levels. Positioned epistemologically alongside scientific laws such as gravity, DNA, and the periodic table, the BB-OS provides a common language for integrating diverse management practices. The article concludes by inviting the academic community to test, refute, replicate, or extend the model through empirical studies.

title: The Impact of Product Placement and Promotions on Consumer Behavior: An Analysis Using the SAI Model

detail.title: The Impact of Product Placement and Promotions on Consumer Behavior: An Analysis Using the SAI Model
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how commodity placement and promotional strategies influence consumer behavior and sales performance. Using the "Sales-Appearance-Impact Model" (SAI = SU × A × R), which integrates sales uplift (SU), rate of product appearance (A), and market reaction (R), the study quantifies the effect of different promotional strategies. Real-world cases from J.C. Penney, Target, Apple, and Red Bull illustrate the spectrum of promotion effectiveness, from low-impact campaigns to extreme, globally recognized marketing events. Findings show that strategic placement and high-visibility promotions substantially increase sales and market presence, while ineffective campaigns yield minimal or negative results. The model provides a practical, data-driven framework for companies to assess and optimize promotional strategies, linking marketing decisions directly to measurable consumer and sales outcomes.

detail.abstract: With the effects of climate change becoming more evident every year, preventing and, ideally, reversing it is a pressing challenge. The Paris Agreement was a milestone in the fight against climate change, establishing a series of specific targets for 2050. The agreement sets out various goals, including to hold the increase in the global temperature to below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit the increase to 1.5°C. Assessing the world’s progress towards this goal requires forward-looking information on the transition to net-zero of countries, companies and the financial sector. In this paper, we begin by highlighting the importance of forward-looking indicators for assessing climate-related transition risks, both for corporations and countries. We then assess a range of currently available data sources, which provide a variety of indicators, particularly for corporations. However, we find that results vary depending on the data sources used, and only a limited number of firms, primarily large ones, are currently disclosing forward-looking indicators. These discrepancies can partly be attributed to differences in methodology, they are not always easy to understand, nor are they always comparable or communicated transparently. Therefore, their appropriate use depends on specific use cases. We also analyse the goals and pathways established by countries to achieve the Paris Agreement’s main target to limit the increase in global temperature through different data sources and frameworks. We find that there are different approaches based on the original goals set by each country with different coverage. We close the paper by outlining potential ways forward for central banks and ways by which statisticians, standard setters and other relevant stakeholders, including private entities, can help improve the quality, accessibility and comparability of forward-looking climate transition risk data.

detail.abstract: Sustainable change is produced via the integration of a vision with a plan, incentives, resources, and skills. The omission of any one of these five elements results, respectively, in confusion, treadmills, resistance, frustration, and anxiety. Many change initiatives are unsustainable not only because one or more of the five key elements are omitted but because the vision is insufficient to the task. Advanced complex systems dynamics modeling transforms how sustainable change initiatives are envisioned and planned, affording new possibilities for success. How, then, might a sustainable career success initiative be informed by advanced modeling principles? Such an initiative is conceived in terms of a mathematical model coordinating and aligning educational and career development opportunities. The model implements measurements of fourteen ability, knowledge, skill, and work activity domains pertaining to over 900 job titles included in the U. S. Department of Labor’s Occupational Information Network (O*NET). A complex system dynamics model based on the O*NET data incorporated into a smartphone app could enable multiple sectors of end users (students, job seekers, educators, career counselors, employees, employers, HR personnel, researchers, labor economists, accountants, investors, legal and regulatory advisors, standards groups, etc.) to envision, plan, incentivize, resource, and skill their complementary perspectives on successful career development trajectories. The Career Success Initiative (CSI) app would coordinate the various stakeholder sectors’ capacities for measuring and managing continuous education and career growth over the span of individuals’ working lives, where the alliances enable each sector to fulfill its goals more effectively than they could in isolation. A significant consequence of this project would be the illumination of a method of devising standards for efficient human capital markets. Extending existing practices in manufactured capital markets, the CSI provides a model for how organizations providing educational, professional development, human resource management, recruitment, and other services could cooperate in setting standards for common product definitions, thereby expanding market size, easing the identification of customers, lowering transaction costs, and enhancing potentials for enhanced profitability stemming from innovative approaches to producing outcomes at lower cost and higher quality. Given these results, insights emerge as to how advanced mathematical modeling of sustainable change initiatives might lead to similarly structured efficient markets for other forms of human, social, and natural capital.

title: The Perils of Excessive Mandatory Disclosure: Balancing Transparency, Agency Costs, and Economic Efficiency in Corporate Law

detail.title: The Perils of Excessive Mandatory Disclosure: Balancing Transparency, Agency Costs, and Economic Efficiency in Corporate Law
detail.abstract: This research paper critically examines the implications of excessive mandatory disclosure in corporate law, challenging the notion that increased transparency invariably prevents wrongdoing and enhances market efficiency. Drawing on key scholarly works, it argues that overbroad disclosure requirements can lead to information overload, resource misallocation, and deadweight losses. The analysis further highlights necessary conditions for effective disclosure, emphasising standardised, objective historical data to mitigate agency costs and information asymmetry, while cautioning against burdensome ESG reporting and unquantifiable metrics. Methodological challenges in policy evaluation are addressed, advocating empirical tools like principal component regression and natural experiments to test causal effects while accounting for reflexivity and endogeneity. The paper concludes that balanced disclosure rules, grounded in economic theory, are essential to optimise social welfare without fostering regulatory overreach.

detail.abstract: The Localization Law (Republic Act [RA] 8190) aims to improve educational equity by emphasizing the recruitment of teachers from local communities, promoting cultural congruence, and reducing relocation expenses. Although RA 8190 has been in effect since 1996, challenges in filling teacher vacancies persist. This study employed a descriptive qualitative research design, using document analysis, key informant interviews, and focus group discussions with school administrators and teachers to assess the law's effectiveness and efficiency. Results highlighted that the law has evolved over time to establish a clear geographic hiring hierarchy while balancing local preference with subject specialization needs, particularly for priority programs supported by mechanisms like transfer priority and teacher ranking. Its implementation reveals significant limitations, such as mismatches in teacher specialization, prolonged recruitment procedures, and a lack of effective monitoring and assessment mechanisms. The observed inconsistencies significantly affected teacher applicants and the school-level hiring and recruitment processes. This necessitates further improvement in the implementation of the law to enhance its effectiveness and efficiency. Therefore, it is essential to amend the law to ensure that its practice is monitored and evaluated to address the current challenges.

title: Progressive User Fess
affiliations: University of Southern California Gould School of Law

detail.title: Progressive User Fess
detail.abstract:
Since the Tax Revolt of the 1970s, cash-strapped state and local governments have increasingly relied on user fees to pay for public programs. Scholars attuned to city budgets raised alarms about these fees. They undermine government's redistributive role, impose regressive costs, and exclude low-income people from vital public services. This Article complicates these prevailing claims based on the first comprehensive study of user fee policies in a sample of American cities.

The Article reveals that policymakers regularly call on a well-known progressive tool to reduce fees' harms: fee waivers. User fees are thus more redistributive than the standard understanding of them has allowed. But they are also more complex. The survey finds that fee waiver eligibility rules are often patchwork, burdensome, and narrowly targeted. User fees form a multifaceted tapestry of exclusion and protection, scarcity and generosity.

The Article also sounds a clarion call: User fees' protective features are not guaranteed. Without adequate defense, fee waivers risk succumbing to external attack from those who would outlaw them. Without adequate scrutiny, they risk falling victim to their own internal design flaws. The Article addresses these risks by offering reform principles drawn from model programs across the country. Mayors, city councils, school boards, and state legislatures can use this Article as a playbook to inform the design of user fees that raise revenue while protecting vulnerable American households.

title: How Much Do International Stocks Move Together: Correlation, Dispersion and Predictability
affiliations: University of Stirling

detail.title: How Much Do International Stocks Move Together: Correlation, Dispersion and Predictability
detail.abstract: This paper considers both correlations and dispersion across a range of (48) international stock market returns. The paper also considers the links with key macroeconomic variables and thus, is informative as to the nature of risk and the interaction between the financial and real economies. While correlations have risen over the sample, as commonly observed, evidence suggests a greater dichotomy in the post-Covid-19 period. In seeking to understand correlation movement, inflation plays a greater role compared to growth, except for the markets of East Europe. Moreover, a negative relation implies that higher inflation leads to investors switching between markets. Differences are again noted for East Europe as well as the GCC region. Evidence of predictability arising from cross-sectional returns dispersion is missing in linear regressions, but is revealed through a Markov-switching approach, with coefficients of opposite signs across market phases. Again, linking to macroeconomic variables suggests that higher dispersion acts as a proxy for risk and indicates weaker future economic conditions. Overall, the results in the paper link market and economic risk factors. Where higher correlations imply a lessening of diversification opportunities (market risk), higher inflation typically results in investors looking to adjust portfolios (falling correlations), although this is not universal across markets. Dispersion acts as an economic risk factor implying changes in subsequent economic performance.

detail.abstract: This study compares labor market outcomes in Spain and South Korea between 2000 and 2022, focusing on the interaction between education attainment, research and development (R&D) investment, and employment performance. Using harmonized OECD and World Bank datasets, the analysis combines unemployment and employment rates, tertiary education attainment, and R&D expenditure into a series of comparative visualizations. The findings reveal a paradox: Spain consistently reports one of the highest rates of tertiary education attainment in Europe yet suffers from persistently high unemployment and low employment rates. South Korea, with slightly lower tertiary education levels, sustains stronger labor market performance. The key difference lies in innovation intensity, Korea invests nearly five percent of GDP in R&D, while Spain invests less than 1.5 percent. The results suggest that education alone is insufficient to ensure labor market resilience; complementary investment in innovation is crucial for translating human capital into employment opportunities.

title: Life or Death: Why India Must Choose Reform Over Retribution
affiliations: Amity University Lucknow Campus

detail.title: Life or Death: Why India Must Choose Reform Over Retribution
detail.abstract: This research paper discusses the criminal justice system in India and that it should focus on reformative justice and consequently not depend on retributive resolution offered by capital punishment. Although capital punishment stands on the books in apposite offences, executions are extremely rare and indicate a major disarray between intent and implementation. The paper suggests that retributive measures do not pass the moral and utilitarian standards. In Section I, the work outlines the present death-penalty system and legal framework in India, the right to life guaranteed under the Indian constitution, and then the Supreme courts doctrine of capital punishment which states the capital punishment should be awarded in the rarest of the rare cases. Section II presents the arguments to the issues of the deterrence effect of the death penalty, arbitrariness, and social bias. Section III contrasts India and the jurisdictions of Nepal, South Africa, and Europe where the constitutional courts have struck down capital punishment. Section IV provides the synthesis of the collected empirical evidence and the theoretical input, stating that the available literature indisputably shows that no credible deterrence influence of executions is found and that most of the death-row prisoners in India are either impoverished or marginalized within the society. Other reforms proposed in the section include juvenile justice bills, sentencing standards, and better punishment conditions in jail.

title: Heterogeneous responses to monetary policy: the role of floating rate loans

detail.title: Heterogeneous responses to monetary policy: the role of floating rate loans
detail.abstract: This study examines the floating rate channel—a mechanism through which monetary policy affects firms’ investment and credit demand based on their exposure to variable rate loans. Using a granular loan-level dataset from the euro area, we find that firms with variable rate loans significantly reduce their investment-related borrowing after monetary tightening, compared to firms with fixed rate loans. This effect is most pronounced among the smallest firms, consistent with the theoretical view that the floating rate channel is explained by financial constraints. Our results highlight the heterogeneity in firms’ reactions to interest rate changes and underscore the importance of accounting for firm size and financial constraints in monetary policy analysis.

detail.abstract: This article investigates the paradox of obedience without command in predictive societies. Authority, once tied to explicit orders and visible command structures, is now embedded in syntactic operations that organize compliance without issuing instructions. Obedience Without Command explores how predictive systems generate silent authority, where rules are followed not because they are commanded, but because their form leaves no alternative. Through case studies of financial reporting, automated governance, and predictive scoring, the paper develops a framework to understand authority that operates without decision-makers, and obedience that emerges without command.

detail.abstract: From sea level rise to extreme weather events and heatwaves, climate impacts are threatening the world's infrastructure in myriad ways. How do infrastructure planners prepare for and invest in infrastructure in the face of this new scientific uncertainty? This Chapter addresses the complex legal, policy, and ethical challenges associated with infrastructure planning and management in the era of climate change. Longstanding infrastructure planning practices that may have worked for a more stable "Earth 1.0" will prove unworkable for an uncertain, climate-destabilized "Earth 2.0." This Chapter addresses three different adaptation strategies available to infrastructure planners: (1) resisting climate impacts by building sea walls and armoring the shoreline; (2) accommodating those impacts by elevating existing structures; and (3) retreating, such as systematically moving people out of harm's way. This Chapter concludes by offering several principles to help guide infrastructure planning efforts during a time of climate-driven destabilization.

detail.abstract: The second presidency of Donald Trump, often referred to as "Trump 2.0," presents significant challenges to the Liberal International Order (LIO), a system of global governance established in the mid-20th century to promote peace, stability, and prosperity through multilateral cooperation. This article examines how Trump's assertive and protectionist "America First" doctrine threatens the foundational principles of the LIO. Key aspects include the United States’ retreat from multilateralism through withdrawals from agreements like the Paris Climate Agreement and the World Health Organization, along with economic nationalism demonstrated by imposing high tariffs on imports from Mexico, Canada, and China. Additionally, Trump's antagonistic approach toward NATO and preference for authoritarian leaders such as Viktor Orbán and Vladimir Putin signal a departure from the US’s traditional commitment to democratic alliances. Furthermore, the abandonment of arms control agreements and neglect of climate change initiatives exacerbate global instability. The article concludes that Trump’s policies reflect a fundamental shift away from the US’s traditional role as the principal architect and guarantor of the LIO, potentially leading to the erosion of global stability and encouraging allies to seek alternative security and economic arrangements.

detail.abstract: The 2022 cycle of the OECD's Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) included, for the first time, a global assessment of creative thinking. Released in 2024, the results provide sobering evidence about the preparedness of today's 18and 19-year-olds, the first generation to enter higher education and the workforce in an AI-saturated world. While policymakers frequently describe creativity as the "future-proof" human skill, the PISA data show that one in four OECD students, and more than half of non-OECD students, fail to reach even baseline proficiency. Only a small minority, 11 percent in OECD and 3 percent in non-OECD countries, achieve advanced levels of creative performance. At the same time, performance in mathematics, reading, and science has stagnated or declined across much of the OECD. The convergence of weak creative skills with eroding core literacies highlights a structural gap between education rhetoric and reality. This paper argues that creativity must be understood as the feedstock skill for empowerment in the age of AI. Using the AI Matrix and education empowerment frameworks, it develops a research agenda focused on three priorities: achieving conceptual clarity on what creativity means, identifying pedagogical strategies that deliberately cultivate it, and examining how creativity functions as a strategic defence against the automation of thought and work.

detail.abstract: We introduce outcome uncertainty into a public goods game to examine heterogeneous motivations for costly punishment. In many real-world situations, outcomes do not result solely from individual choices but are affected by uncontrollable factors, making it difficult to infer intentions from outcomes. To reflect this, we introduce random noise to the connection between contributions and payoffs, such that rational free-riding does not always lead to higher earnings, and cooperation does not necessarily result in lower ones. Under this setting, participants must decide whether to punish others based on their contributions, payoffs, or both. We identify four distinct punishment types: some punish low contributors (Type R), others target high earners (Type IA), some display weak patterns (Type S), and others behave inconsistently (Type O). Even among Type R, concerns for payoff inequality persist as a secondary influence. These results suggest that punishment serves not only to promote cooperation but also to correct outcomes perceived as unfair. Since many punitive systems operate through centralized sanctioning authority, understanding these diverse motivations sheds light on what people consider a legitimate basis for punishment. Our findings caution against relying on narrow 1 Springer Nature 2021 L A T E X template 2 Heterogeneous Punishment under Uncertainty assumptions and suggest that simplified interpretations of sanctioning behavior may overlook important concerns about outcome justice.

detail.abstract: This paper reexamines the pluralism of fairness ideals proposed by Cappelen et al. (2007) using our modified estimation models that account for self-interest preferences, specifically egoists. While Cappelen et al. (2007) identified three distinct fairness ideals-strict egalitarianism, libertarianism, and liberal egalitarianism-we introduce models that acknowledge individuals who consistently maximize their own payoffs regardless of fairness, categorizing them as pure egoists. Importantly, even with pure egoists considered as a distinct type, we find that individuals adhering to the three fairness ideals proposed by Cappelen et al. title: Addressing Counterfeiting and Piracy Challenges in Nigeria: The role of Intellectual Property Law

detail.abstract: Counterfeiting and piracy remain one of the most disturbing problems facing Intellectual Property in Nigeria today. From fake drugs in the pharmaceutical sector to pirated music, movies, software, and counterfeit fashion items, the menace has eaten deep into the economy. It not only reduces the profit of genuine business owners but also exposes consumers to dangerous products. This article looks at the effect of counterfeiting and piracy on different industries in Nigeria and examines the role of intellectual property laws in solving these problems. The Nigerian Copyright Commission, the Customs Service, and other agencies have roles in enforcement, but their efforts are limited due to challenges like corruption and lack of resources. The paper then proposes strategies such as stronger collaboration, legislative reform, public sensitization, and international cooperation. In conclusion, it stresses that Nigeria needs to take intellectual property protection more seriously if it wants to grow its economy and protect the lives of citizens.

title: Competition Law and Policy in Crisis and the Rise of the Expansive State

detail.title: Competition Law and Policy in Crisis and the Rise of the Expansive State
detail.abstract: Competition Law and Policy has long been shaped by the Limited State paradigm, which emphasized minimal government intervention and framed competition enforcement as a narrowly focused, technocratic exercise. However, recent crises-including the 2008 Financial Crisis, the coronavirus disease-2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, and geopolitical shifts-have triggered a transition toward the Expansive State. This article makes an original contribution by analysing how the old paradigm shaped Competition Law and Policy, and how its rejection is now challenging the system, necessitating a rethinking of values, priorities, and institutional roles. It argues that beyond traditional enforcement, advocacy must become a core function of competition agencies to ensure competition principles are not overlooked by the Expansive State but remain actively considered in policymaking. The analysis highlights the need to reclaim neglected enforcement areas, address entrenched corporate power, and prevent further market concentration. At the same time, it warns against the risks of political instrumentalization, cautioning against the potential marginalization of Competition Law and Policy. Ultimately, the article calls for an adaptive, forward-looking framework that balances enforcement with evolving public interest considerations, ensuring Competition Law and Policy continues to foster economic dynamism, innovation, and consumer welfare in the Expansive State era.

title: The Death of the Legal Author. Authority, Intention, and Law-Creation in the Advent of GenAI
affiliations: University of Girona and University of Belgrade - Faculty of Law

detail.title: The Death of the Legal Author. Authority, Intention, and Law-Creation in the Advent of GenAI
detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence in the form of chatbots based on large language models (LLMs) has taken the world of law by storm. Philosophy of law is struggling to catch up with the theoretical significance of the advent of technological development and the way it may modify traditionally established understanding of legal phenomena, such as law-creation and authority. In this sense, for the most part, heated philosophical debates have circled around a normative question: "Should AI create and interpret law?". Much less attention has been given to a different, albeit previous, question: "Can AI create and interpret law?" That is, is AI capable of producing outputs that can be deemed as "law" (at least, law as we know it)? Can AI be a "legal author"? This paper explores this unattended question and endeavours to provide some provisional answers. In the first part, we define legal authority, legal authorship, and legal interpretation and claim that the intention of a determinate authoritative author is often considered the condition of the possibility of creating and interpreting contemporary legal texts. In the second part, we argue that LLM AI, in general, and ChatGPT, in particular, generate legal texts without having any intention. In the third part, we consider the positions of the authors that downplay or even eliminate intention from the discussions about the legal character of prescriptive texts. 4. Finally, we argue that there are good reasons to side with the second group of authors. The ability of agents without intentions, like ChatGPT, to create legal text is an argument in favour of the thesis that law can be created without intention behind the creation and that nonintentional creation can be interpreted to arrive at legal norms.

title: Do Institutional Investors’ Environmental Concerns Improve Corporate Environmental Sustainability Practices? A Machine Learning-based Textual Analysis

detail.abstract: Although institutional investors pay attention to environmental issues in listed companies, the impact is rarely studied. Based on the Q&A transcripts of institutional site visits, this paper explores and quantifies the content of institutional investors’ environmental concerns, and explores the subsequent environmental sustainability practices of listed companies and external feedback. Results show that during institutional site visits, institutional investors’ environmental attention has a positive effect on the subsequent environmental sustainability practices of listed companies visited. When the investigated listed companies are non-state-owned enterprises, small and medium-sized enterprises, face high financing constraints, receive low media attention, and do not belong to the new energy industry, the role of institutional investors’ environmental focus in promoting subsequent environmental sustainability practices of these companies can be significantly enhanced. Moreover,  sustainable performance of listed companies will receive positive external evaluation and feedback. This paper provides effective guidance for institutional investors, listed companies and regulatory authorities.

title: Buffer usability in a complex world: Interactions between macroprudential regulation and the resolution framework
