detail.title: Buffer usability in a complex world: Interactions between macroprudential regulation and the resolution framework
detail.abstract: This paper explores the interplay between the risk- and leverage-based prudential and the resolution frameworks within the EU banking system. The prudential framework is designed to enhance the resilience of both individual banks and the banking sector as a whole. It does so by imposing minimum capital requirements and capital buffers that can absorb losses during periods of financial stress. Conversely, the resolution framework focuses on ensuring that banks have adequate loss-absorbing and recapitalisation capacity to facilitate an orderly resolution process, thereby safeguarding public funds. The simultaneous use of capital across and within these two frameworks can have an impact on the effectiveness of capital buffers, presenting various challenges for macroprudential authorities. Our analysis shows that overlaps between risk-based and leverage-based requirements within the prudential framework reduce buffer usability to around 65% to 74% of the overall combined buffer requirement. When the resolution framework is also considered, buffer usability further declines to an average of 40% to 50%, depending on the analytical approach employed. Our simulations of buffer usability under different regulatory options discussed in the literature suggest that implementing the final Basel III standards in the EU would significantly increase buffer usability. The paper also analyses the impact of other options that could reduce or eliminate overlaps between capital buffers and other parallel requirements and quantifies the trade-offs between increased buffer usability and the costs of implementation. As resolution requirements are fully phased in as of 2024, the future evolution of buffer usability and the potential challenges for macroprudential authorities will also depend on how banks set their capital targets relative to the parallel frameworks and how they adapt their balance sheet structures to meet prudential and resolution requirements.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between national tax policy resulting in harmful tax competition and its legality under international law. It begins by outlining the notion of harmful tax competition or tax havens. The paper explores the impact of harmful tax competition on national tax policies and loss of revenue, which further erodes the socio-economic development, protection, and promotion of human rights. The author argues that economic development is a sine qua non for the protection of human rights, and the existence of harmful tax competition results in irreparable loss to the socio-economic development of many countries, especially the developing countries. Since hindrance to socio-economic development ultimately affects the human rights prospects, the authors conclude that the continuation of tax havens is fundamentally against the established rules of International Law.

title: 인구변화가 지역별 노동시장에 미치는 영향 분석 (The Impact of Demographic Change on Regional Labor Markets)

detail.title: 인구변화가 지역별 노동시장에 미치는 영향 분석 (The Impact of Demographic Change on Regional Labor Markets)

publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Korea Economic Research Institute Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Korean Abstract: 이 연구는 장래의 인구변화가 노동시장에 미치는 영향을 살펴보기 위해 2022년부터 2042년까지의 시군구 경제활동인구 변화를 전망하였다. 전망 결과는 장차 인구변화로 인해 시군구 간 경제활동인구 격차가 빠르게 확대된다는 것을 보여준다. 시뮬레이션 분석 결과는 시군구 간 청년층 인구이동의 균등화가 장래 시군구 간 노동인구 불균등 증가 추이를 완화할 것임을 알려준다. 반면, 장년층의 인구이동이 사라지는 경우, 시군구 간 경제활동인구 격차는 더 커질 것으로 예상된다. 전반적인 경제활동참가율 증가는 시군구 경제활동인구 불균등도 변화 추이에 큰 영향을 미치지 못하는 것으로 나타났다. 이러한 결과는 현재와 같은 형태의 지역 간 청년 인구이동 차이를 완화하고 장년 인구이동 차이를 강화하는 정책이 앞으로 시군구 경제활동인구 불균형을 완화할 수 있는 방안임을 보여준다. 전반적인 경제활동참가율 제고만으로는 지역 간 경제활동인구 격차 확대를 막기 어려우며, 지역의 사정에 따라 차별화된 고용정책이 필요하다. 

English Abstract: This study projects changes in the economically active population across cities, counties, and districts in Korea from 2022 to 2042 in order to examine the implications of future demographic shifts for regional labor markets. The projections reveal that demographic change is likely to widen disparities in the economically active population across localities at an accelerating pace. Simulation results further indicate that a more balanced distribution of youth migration across regions could mitigate the trend of increasing inequality in the future working-age population. By contrast, the absence of mobility among the older population would exacerbate disparities in regional labor supply. An overall increase in the labor force participation rate, however, appears to exert only limited influence on the trajectory of regional inequality in the economically active population. These findings suggest that policies designed to reduce interregional disparities in youth migration while reinforcing imbalances in olderage migration could serve as effective measures to ease future imbalances in regional labor supply. Enhancing the overall labor force participation rate alone is unlikely to contain the widening gap, underscoring the need for region-specific employment policies tailored to local circumstances.

title: Rival Definitions of Economic Rent: Historical Origins and Normative Implications

detail.title: Rival Definitions of Economic Rent: Historical Origins and Normative Implications

declarations.funderStatement: Economic and Social Research Council (ESRC)

detail.abstract: Across the political spectrum, the concept of economic rent is used to delegitimise certain incomes by marking them out as unearned and/or inefficient. But too often, users offer either no definition of rent, multiple definitions that are logically incompatible, and/or definitions whose normative implications they appear not to comprehend. The first generalised concept of rent, which gained traction in the late 1800s, referred to incomes analogous to land rents in the sense of rewarding control over persistently scarce or monopolised assets, rather than labour or sacrifice. But by the mid-twentieth century, a very different concept of rent had been widely adopted by neoclassical economists: income in excess of opportunity cost or competitive price. According to this revised concept, most land rents would no longer qualify as rents. This article offers an account of how such rival understandings of rent emerged, evaluates the normative positions embedded within each, and considers why so many commentators fail to spot their incompatibility. It describes how the concept of rent, that the earliest adopters hoped would justify the socialisation of scarce and monopolised assets, became bent out of recognition, and deployed for diametrically opposed purposes.

title: Taking Stock: A Foundation for Future Housing Strategy
affiliations: University College London and

detail.title: Taking Stock: A Foundation for Future Housing Strategy

declarations.funderStatement: Laudes Foundation

detail.abstract:
England’s housing system is failing on multiple fronts. Record levels of homelessness and overcrowding, persistently high rents, deepening wealth inequalities, and homes that are unhealthy and unaffordable to heat are symptoms of a housing system that no longer fulfils its most basic purpose: providing decent, affordable homes for all.

Successive governments have pledged to solve the crisis through large-scale, market- led new-build. The current government is targeting 1.5 million homes by the end of the parliament and making a significant and welcome investment in the social and affordable housing sector. However, the evidence suggests that expanding the housing stock – without addressing deeper structural problems with our housing system – will have only a modest effect on housing affordability. 

Moreover, a business-as-usual reliance on large-scale new construction to address the affordability crisis generates significant greenhouse gas emissions and ecosystem damage and is not compatible with the UK’s climate goals and biodiversity targets. The labour demands of the new-build industry will also exacerbate the shortage of workers available for retrofit, and divert construction sector capacity from other critical sectors, including transport, net-zero and health infrastructure.

Fortunately, our initial analysis suggests there are credible ways both to address the affordability crisis without relying so heavily on new-build and reduce the environmental impact of new construction. These include tapping into the latent capacity within the existing housing stock and making smarter use of policy levers that directly influence the price and distribution of homes. Utilising this broader toolkit will allow us to address housing need more quickly and effectively than relying on new construction alone while, in some cases, reducing costs to the public purse. Such a reorientation of housing policy would also help to free up labour and construction sector capacity to make progress where it is also urgently needed: in retrofit. 

Taking Stock is the first output of Homes that Don’t Cost the Earth, an initiative led by Arup, Dark Matter Labs, Rising Tide and UCL Institute for Innovation and Public Purpose (IIPP). Homes that Don’t Cost the Earth aims to identify the changes in English housing policy and practice that could enable us to meet housing needs within environmental limits and real resource constraints. Taking Stock outlines the foundational analysis that will guide the next stages of our work, including the framework and metrics we propose to use to evaluate housing policy and practice, and the key areas where we believe change is both necessary and possible.

title: Nuevos elementos para el debate sobre el bien jurídico libre competencia ("New Elements for the Debate on the Legal Interest Protected by Competition Law”)

detail.abstract:
A 30 años de la dictación del Decreto Ley 211, de 1973, que fija normas para la defensa de la libre competencia (DL 211), se le han efectuado reformas mediante la Ley 19.911, de 2003, dentro de las cuales está la relativa al bien jurídico -la libre competencia- que se establece expresamente en el artículo 1° DL 211. La importancia del bien jurídico existente detrás de las leyes de competencia se debe al catálogo ejemplar que contemplan las diversas legislaciones sobre conductas anticompetitivas, entre ellas la chilena, que entrega insuficiente certeza a los agentes económicos en su actuar; y también a la necesidad de un criterio que guíe el juicio del Tribunal de Defensa de la Libre Competencia (TDLC), respecto al conocimiento de prácticas contrarias a la competencia.

Abstract: Thirty years after the enactment of Decree Law 211 of 1973, which sets forth rules for the defense of competition (DL 211), it was amended in 2003 by Law 19,911 including a reform concerning the legal interest—free competition—now expressly established in Article 1 of DL 211. The importance of the legal interest underlying competition laws lies in the exemplary catalogue of anticompetitive conducts provided by various legislations, including the Chilean one, which offers insufficient certainty to economic agents in their actions; as well as in the need for a guiding criterion for the judgment of the Tribunal de Defensa de la Libre Competencia (TDLC) when adjudicating practices contrary to competition.

detail.abstract: In the context of the rapidly evolving innovation ecosystems across Africa, this study investigates the advanced application of Markov chains as a robust analytical framework for modeling probabilistic transitions between various stages of entrepreneurial development. By integrating empirical data enriched with contextual variables, such as technological adoption, access to financing, and the influence of public policies, the research offers a dynamic and systemic perspective on the trajectories of African startups. The proposed approach identifies critical stages within the entrepreneurial lifecycle and outlines strategic levers aimed at guiding both institutional and private actors in enhancing support mechanisms for innovation.

title: Stochastic thermodynamics of financial markets I: entropy production and the second law.
affiliations: GammaDynamics, LLC

detail.title: Stochastic thermodynamics of financial markets I: entropy production and the second law.
detail.abstract:
We consider the total entropy change of a financial market as a sum of the environment (medium) entropy change and the particle (market) entropy change. The sum measures how much is already priced-in the market. The first summand measures the exchange of "heat" between the market and its environment. In order to simplify it, we introduce the "irreversibility drift": its average square is proportional to the total entropy change.

We estimate these quantities from the data and demonstrate experimentally that the total entropy change (the average total entropy production) is non-negative, as required by the second law of thermodynamics.

It focuses on retail CBDCs and examines the legal framework for implementing them in selected jurisdictions, concentrating on governance and risk distribution. It then considers adoption challenges and opportunities for commercial banks and individuals, followed by the legal dimensions of public awareness necessary to facilitate the adoption of a retail CBDC. It concludes by providing an international dimension on using retail CBDCs to settle cross-border retail payments.

title: A Nascent International Financial Channel of China's Monetary Policy Transmission
affiliations: Fudan University - International School of Finance (FISF), Johns Hopkins University - Carey Business School and University of Macau - Faculty of Business Administration

detail.title: A Nascent International Financial Channel of China's Monetary Policy Transmission
detail.abstract: Chinese private portfolio equity outflows, though small compared to other Chinese outflows, are growing rapidly because of capital account liberalization and capital flight. Using granular stock-holding data on Qualified Domestic Institutional Investor (QDII) mutual funds, we identify a nascent financial channel of international transmission of Chinese monetary policy to world stocks. Event study analysis around monetary policy announcement days reveals that monetary policy tightening depresses returns of country equity indexes and individual U.S. stocks with QDII fund exposure relative to non-exposed stocks. The results are robust to controlling for the real transmission channel of Chinese monetary policy and other confounders. The effect is driven by smaller and less liquid firms, but not by China-concept stocks or those highly exposed to China's macroeconomic shocks. We also find that the results are driven by household portfolio rebalancing from more to less risky assets following the announcement.

title: The GENIUS Act and Stablecoin Adoption in 2025: Legal, Computational, and Financial Stability Perspectives

authors.first_name: Prof. Ts. Dr. MD Asri bin

affiliations: , Universiti Teknologi Malaysia, Malaysia, Universiti Teknologi Malaysia, Malaysia and Universiti Teknologi Malaysia, Malaysia

detail.title: The GENIUS Act and Stablecoin Adoption in 2025: Legal, Computational, and Financial Stability Perspectives

keywords: Stablecoin Regulation GENIUS Act; MiCA Regulation; Monte Carlo Simulation; Financial Stability.

detail.abstract: The paper evaluates the regulatory, financial, and technological implications of the U.S. Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act (GENIUS Act), enacted in 2025, and its potential impact on stablecoin adoption and systemic stability. Drawing on a diffusion of innovation model, a Monte Carlo redemption stress test, and a comparative legal analysis with the European Union’s Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) Regulation, the study provides one of the first integrated assessments of stablecoin regulation across law, computation, and finance. Results demonstrate that the GENIUS framework accelerates adoption by embedding stablecoin issuance within the U.S. banking system, producing a credibility premium relative to MiCA. Adoption is projected to reach 50 per cent of the potential market within six years under GENIUS, compared to eleven years under MiCA. However, stress-testing reveals material fragility: redemption shocks generate failure probabilities exceeding 8 per cent even with conservative reserve ratios, underscoring the vulnerability of blockchain-enabled bank runs. The legal matrix further highlights GENIUS’s prioritization of rapid domestic integration over consumer protection and cross-border harmonization. The findings identify a regulatory paradox: credibility accelerates adoption, but without explicit liquidity backstops, statutory redemption rights, and international coordination, it also accelerates fragility. Policy recommendations include conditional access to Federal Reserve liquidity, transatlantic coordination of reserve standards, activity-based oversight of DeFi markets, and strengthened consumer protections. The paper contributes to the emerging literature by offering a comprehensive, interdisciplinary evaluation of stablecoin regulation, providing actionable insights for policymakers seeking to balance innovation with financial stability in the digital era.

title: Does Better Information Drive Better Seed Choices? Experimental Evidence from Kenya
affiliations: CIMMYT Kenya, CIMMYT Kenya, CIMMYT Kenya, International Maize and Wheat Improvement Centre, CIMMYT Kenya and International Maize and Wheat Improvement Centre

detail.title: Does Better Information Drive Better Seed Choices? Experimental Evidence from Kenya
detail.abstract: Despite advances in hybrid maize performance in Kenya, many farmers continue planting varieties released over two decades ago. Farmer experimentation with and use of relatively newer hybrids is crucial to improve regional food security, especially amid the increasing pressures of climate change. This study uses a randomized controlled trial to assess the degree to which contextually relevant and product-specific performance information influences farmer seed choice. Farmers in the treatment group received yield data for ten hybrids grown by farmers in the previous growing season in their county, while those in the control group received placebo information unrelated to seed selection. The intervention tripled farmers' intent to buy top-performing hybrids (from 7% to 27%) and more than doubled actual purchases (from 5% to 13%). Stockouts prevented some intended purchases, but treated farmers were still more likely to choose these hybrids. This study highlights a critical gap: farmers tend to lack independent and credible up-todate information on seed performance. Investing in rigorous testing of currently available hybrids and improving how results are shared with farmers can help address this issue. Providing credible performance data can support better decision-making, speed up varietal turnover, and strengthen seed systems in Kenya and beyond.

title: Online Platforms Provide Access to Valid Eastern Samples

detail.title: Online Platforms Provide Access to Valid Eastern Samples

declarations.ethicsApproval: Thhis study has been approved by three institutional review boards: Committee for Protection of Human Subjects (CPHS) and Office for Protection of Human Subjects (OPHS) at University of California, Berkeley; NYU WSQ (New York University Washington Square IRB); and Institutional Review Board at CUHKSZ (The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen).

detail.abstract: Western-centered (primarily American-centered) samples have long faced criticism, yet limited progress has been made to address this issue. The present research validates data from an Eastern culture—China—offering a promising solution. We conducted 11 preregistered studies with 18,256 Chinese and American online participants, examining well-established phenomena across various social science disciplines. The findings provide strong evidence that Chinese online platforms offer geographically and demographically diverse samples from across China. These participants are highly attentive and produce valid data. Additionally, we find tentative evidence that language is a surmountable barrier for Western researchers, as translation variations had little impact on Chinese participants’ responses in our tests. Finally, we share practical insights on using Chinese online platforms for data collection. We hope this paper encourages researchers to embrace diverse samples by trying them in their own research and appreciating it in the research of others.

title: Firm-Level Political Risk and Systemic Risk: The Role of Board Interlocks and Corporate Political Activity
affiliations: Independent and Indian Institute of Management Indore

detail.title: Firm-Level Political Risk and Systemic Risk: The Role of Board Interlocks and Corporate Political Activity
detail.abstract: We investigate the effect of firm-level political risk on systemic risk contribution. Using a 20-year firm-quarter panel of 5445 US-listed firms, we document a significantly positive association between firm-level political and systemic risks. The results remain consistent with a battery of robustness tests, propensity score matching, and instrumental variable analysis by mitigating any endogeneity concerns. We identify two potential non-business channels which may exacerbate this association. First, consistent with the literature on board interlocks, which provides evidence of information transmission and diffusion of corporate practices across firms, we find the positive association between political risk and systemic risk to be amplified in the presence of strong board connections. Next, we examine the role of corporate political activity, specifically lobbying and political campaign contributions. We find evidence that corporate political activity magnifies the association between political risk and systemic risk. Firms occupying influential positions within the lobbying and campaign contribution networks exhibit a pronounced effect of political risk on systemic risk. Our study provides novel insights into the systemic importance of firm-level political risk.

title: Who is a central bank for? The founding and legal design of the Bank of Canada

detail.title: Who is a central bank for? The founding and legal design of the Bank of Canada

declarations.funderStatement: Funding support for this article was provided by the Canada Program of the Weatherhead Center for International Affairs at Harvard University and the Osgoode Society for Canadian Legal History R. Roy McMurtry Fellowship.

detail.abstract: The Bank of Canada is an independent Crown corporation that sees its primary responsibility to be promoting Canada's economic welfare by maintaining low and stable inflation. When it was first created in 1934, however, the Bank was a radically different institution-a privately owned corporation primarily meant to anchor Canada's economy globally and manage foreign exchange. Not only was the Bank not tasked with managing inflation, but key policymakers behind its founding thought doing so would be a severe mistake. This article offers the first legal history of the Bank's founding. It maps the enormous public debate that accompanied the creation of the Bank and the various, often contradictory visions expressed for it. The article labels these five visions: a Bankers' Bank, a Government Bank, an Imperial Bank, an Economists' Bank, and a Bank of the People. The article then looks at the original legal design of the Bank and argues that it largely fit the Imperial Bank model. Charting this history helps us better understand this vital organ of Canadian government, and has the potential to upset many of our accepted, contemporary notions of central banking.

title: The Public-Private Dichotomy in Executive Office: A Critical Analysis of Travel Expenditure and the Erosion of Public Trust in Sri Lankan Politics
affiliations: Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology

detail.title: The Public-Private Dichotomy in Executive Office: A Critical Analysis of Travel Expenditure and the Erosion of Public Trust in Sri Lankan Politics
detail.abstract: This paper examines the blurred boundary between private and official conduct within executive power, focusing on recent allegations against former Sri Lankan President Ranil Wickremesinghe. The misappropriation of public funds for travel blending personal and state purposes presents a significant challenge to accountability. Using a qualitative analysis guided by Saliya's (2021a, 2021b) Integrated-Flexible Approach (IFA), the study contextualizes presidential travel expenditures (2010-2025) within the broader framework of institutional integrity and public trust. The analysis invokes the metaphor of a "point of no return" where ambiguous ethical standards irreversibly erode civic confidence. Findings suggest that the absence of transparent, codified rules for official travel fosters selective outrage and partisan exploitation. To prevent further accountability collapse, the study recommends codified legislative rules, independent oversight, and mandatory transparency to distinguish between good-faith official duties and malfeasance. The analysis also highlights how cross-partisan elite solidarity, often disguised as compassion, further undermines accountability by shielding political actors from genuine scrutiny.

title: Administrative Obstruction in EU Education: Institutional Hypocrisy and Rule-of-Law Deficiency at Semmelweis University. Third Part of Administrative Obstruction in EU Education: A Legal Case from Semmelweis University

detail.abstract: This paper is the fifth installment in the series concerning Administrative Obstruction in EU Education. Building upon earlier case studies, including issues related to denial of access, inadequacies in specimen handling, assessment bias, and systemic over-enrollment, this study critically examines the institutional hypocrisy revealed by Semmelweis University's public stance towards the European Commission. On December 18, 2024, the University issued an official statement protesting the ongoing application of Council Implementing Decision (EU) 2022/2506 by the Commission. The statement referenced principles of fairness, due process, and the right to be heard. However, documented evidence shows that Semmelweis University systematically impairs these fundamental rights in its treatment of students. This article contextualizes these contradictions within the framework of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights and the European Commission's December 2024 Resolution (C(2024) 9140 final). It asserts that the European Commission's evaluation of Hungary's "not yet suitable" remedial measures should additionally account for micro-level deficiencies in university governance, which reflect the very rule-of-law issues identified at the national level.

title: Separating Positive Impact from Warm Glow: Implications for Fund Managers, Educators, Financial Advisers, Rating Agencies, and Investors
affiliations: Santa Clara University - Department of Finance

detail.title: Separating Positive Impact from Warm Glow: Implications for Fund Managers, Educators, Financial Advisers, Rating Agencies, and Investors
detail.abstract:
The ecosystem we now call sustainability investing has always had positive impact and warm glow as its components. Yet in recent decades a false claim has emerged whereby investors can create positive impact while enjoying warm glow by excluding from their portfolio companies violating their values or including companies supporting their values. Some even claim that investors can do well while doing good, earning higher than market returns.

I argue that it is time to stand against these false claims and separate once again positive impact from warm glow. I describe what separation and regrouping would require of fund managers, educators, financial advisers, rating agencies, and investors.

title: Exploring the Heckscher-Ohlin Theory Again: World Trade Structure, Factor Demand Law, and General Trade Equilibrium
affiliations: Mountain State University

detail.title: Exploring the Heckscher-Ohlin Theory Again: World Trade Structure, Factor Demand Law, and General Trade Equilibrium
detail.abstract: Ohlin believed that factor price equalization should show the relationship between factor supply and factor prices. Guo (2023) presented the general price-trade equilibrium of the Heckscher-Ohlin model, which explored the connection between factor supplies and their prices. This development needs further expansion, validation, and discussion. Therefore, this study verifies the logic and reasoning behind equilibrium to explain its properties, especially gains from trade, autarky prices, world trade structure, and comparative advantages. The study shows that equilibrium refines the most proportional relationships in the H-O theory into functional relationships and adds a new aspect to the theory. It highlights the importance of Helpman and Krugman's (1985) trade volumes in shaping the world trade structure, which illustrates the extent and share of a country's exports in international trade. The study serves as a useful complement to the factor price equalization theorem.

title: Behavioral Economics in High School Markets --Decoy Effect and the Profit Function
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Behavioral Economics in High School Markets --Decoy Effect and the Profit Function

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The research aim to find out the effectiveness of decoy effect in high school settings. The experiment was designed to increase the sale of schools merchandise in order to boost school spirits around the community,
declarations.ethicsApproval: This is not a social study experiment, therefore there's no ethical issues
declarations.funderStatement: Catlin Gabel school funded the research, and provided the products the experiment used in the sale.

detail.abstract: This research explores how behavioral economics theories, particularly the Decoy Effect, can be applied to real-life sales strategies within a high school setting. Conducted at Catlin Gabel School, the experiment tested merchandise pricing strategies by introducing a decoy item that aimed to dominate students' purchasing behavior. Sales data showed a significant increase from 23% to 78% in target purchases when the decoy was present. To quantify this effect, a profit function model was developed using key variables: original purchase probability (q₀), adjusted probability under influence (q₁), and decoy detection probability (δ). The findings highlight how consumer choices can be shaped by pricing structures and support the use of behavioral economics in school-based or small business sales planning. Limitations of decoy effect and future applications are discussed.

title: Operationalising Ethical AI Governance - Challenges in Applying Ethical Guidelines Within Organisational Contexts as Actionable Governance Structures

detail.title: Operationalising Ethical AI Governance - Challenges in Applying Ethical Guidelines Within Organisational Contexts as Actionable Governance Structures
detail.abstract: This paper continues researching the challenges that hinder implementation of ethical governance of AI technologies within organizations, emphasizing the disconnect between overarching ethical guidelines and their operationalization within governance structures. Drawing on a qualitative synthesis of academic and industry literature, the paper documents three main categories of barriers: organizational, regulatory, and technical (Morley et al., 2023; Gupta, 2022). Examples of organizational barriers include lack of clearly defined leadership, insufficient executive involvement, and siloed leadership. Regulatory barriers include lack of consistency in legal frameworks and vague compliance requirements. Technical barriers include lack of explainability, inadequate data, and problems with data merging. Findings show that in addition to these barriers, there are interdependent barriers, which form systems of stagnation that slow the advance of ethically-aligned AI systems. The paper provides actionable insights for policymakers, corporate leaders, and AI ethics compliance officers, encouraging proactive and effective governance that translates ethical commitments into legally bound structures, and enhances stakeholder confidence in AI systems and algorithmic governance within the organizational decision-making processes.

title: Digital Piracy and OTT Platforms: Is Current Copyright Law Sufficient?
affiliations: Nirma University, Institute of Law and Nirma University, Institute of Law

detail.title: Digital Piracy and OTT Platforms: Is Current Copyright Law Sufficient?
detail.abstract: The post-pandemic era has transformed the global entertainment landscape, with Over-the-Top (OTT) platforms such as Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+ Hotstar emerging as primary modes of content consumption. However, this growth has been paralleled by an alarming rise in digital piracy, which undermines not only revenues but also the integrity of intellectual property rights. Piracy networks today exploit anonymity, cross-border hosting, and consumer demand for free access, distributing content within minutes of its official release. India’s legal framework, anchored in the Copyright Act, 1957 and reinforced by the IT Rules, 2021, has attempted to address these challenges through dynamic injunctions, John Doe orders, and criminal action. Courts, particularly the Delhi High Court, have displayed commendable creativity in adapting to the speed of infringement, yet enforcement remains reactive and fragmented. A comparative look at global regimes highlights the effectiveness of the U.S. Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), the European Union’s proactive content filters, and international coalitions like the Alliance for Creativity and Entertainment (ACE). The blog concludes that India must pursue a holistic approach strengthening legal mechanisms, embracing technological innovation, fostering cross-border cooperation, and reshaping consumer attitudes in order to effectively safeguard creativity and sustain the promise of the OTT revolution.

title: Attributing Behavior, Knowledge, and Intent -Principles, Rules, and Questions for Software and AI Law
affiliations: European University Viadrina Frankfurt (Oder) - European New School of Digital Studies and European University Viadrina Frankfurt (Oder) - European New School of Digital Studies

detail.title: Attributing Behavior, Knowledge, and Intent -Principles, Rules, and Questions for Software and AI Law
detail.abstract:
Are AI agents legal agents? This chapter examines how the law should attribute actions, knowledge, and intent to software and AI systems that increasingly operate with autonomy. It argues that the decisive legal criterion is whether a system has been delegated authority to act with legal significance absent real-time human sign-off. When such autonomy exists, machines should be treated as agents rather than mere tools, and their outputs must be attributed to principals under doctrines parallel to those governing human agents. This approach prevents liability gaps, deters evasion of responsibility, and aligns accountability with the autonomy risk assumed by deployers. 

The chapter analyzes attribution of actions, cognitive states, and volitional states, highlighting both doctrinal foundations and policy implications. It advances a functional framework of strict but tailored attribution, subject to limited exceptions, and proposes mechanisms such as statutory principles, proportional liability, and conditional safe harbors. By codifying thresholds for attribution and adapting them to technological features, the law can preserve coherence, foster innovation, and ensure effective redress in an era of autonomous software and AI agents.

The rapid advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) are transforming numerous sectors, particularly biotechnology, where AI systems now play an active role in autonomous research and invention generation. This paper introduces, for the first time, the universal model of augmented invention—a hybrid legal category recognizing patentable outputs co-produced by human agents and AI under meaningful human oversight—and examines its implications for patent law in the biosciences.
Focusing on inventorship, ownership, and patentability, the paper highlights the need to adapt patent frameworks to reflect AI’s accelerating impact on research timelines and innovation processes. It analyzes the economic incentives and ethical dimensions of AI-generated inventions, including equity, access, and accountability challenges, and proposes targeted reforms: statutory recognition of augmented inventorship, AI-specific disclosure requirements, and adaptive compulsory licensing triggers. These reforms aim to ensure that patent law both fosters technological progress and safeguards the public interest.

title: Understanding Why People Value Working from Home or Hybrid Workplace Flexibility

detail.title: Understanding Why People Value Working from Home or Hybrid Workplace Flexibility
detail.abstract: As Working-From-Home (WFH) practices expanded rapidly to limit viral spread during the COVID-19 pandemic and continued into the pandemic recovery period, most debates over WFH turned towards discussing productivity rather than the reasons for WFH or flexibility. This study investigates why individuals value WFH/hybrid work arrangements in the US. Understanding why individuals desire WFH or hybrid work arrangements can facilitate constructive and effective negotiations and yield better solutions for employers, such as an increase in productivity, as well as facilitating work-life balance or the incorporation of caregiving or other priorities for employees. Reasons that employees desire WFH or flexible work location arrangements are heterogenous; while the majority of the public debate has focused on whether or not employers should or should not allow WFH the numerous and varying reasons for desiring flexibility have been largely overlooked. Using data from a nationally representative online survey conducted in late 2021, a best-worst scaling experiment was used to elicited rank ordered motivations for remote work. Results reveal the most valued reason for WFH is balancing work with caregiving responsibilities, followed by reducing commuting time and costs, limiting exposure to illness, and preferring the home environment. A latent class model identifies four unobserved heterogeneous preference segments of respondents, namely groups focused on caregiving and commuting, productivity and comfort, multitasking with health safety, and a diffuse group with no strong top reason for WFH flexibility. Additionally, seemingly unrelated regression analysis links WFH preferences with behavioral changes in grooming, attire, and personal care. These findings offer nuanced insights into employee priorities, guiding organizations in designing flexible work policies that align productivity goals with employee well-being.

detail.title: Exploring the Legal and Ethical Implications of Copyright in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
detail.abstract:
In the rapidly evolving age of Artificial intelligence (AI), the convergence of technology and
copyright law, presents numerous intricate legal and ethical implications. It is however pertinent
to note that with the rapid evolution of AI, it has brought about series of questions and debates
about the ownership of creations generated by autonomous systems, the extent of copyright
protection and the balance between encouraging innovations and promoting access to
knowledge. This Project delves deep into the changing landscape of Copyright law as it concerns
and relates to Artificial Intelligence, focusing on key areas of contention and debate. It succinctly
examines the issue of Authorship, Attribution, plagiarism and fair usage which arises when AI
systems autonomously generate creative works such as literature, music or visual art. Right from
time, traditional copyright laws attribute authorship to human creators, but with the rapid growth
of AI, the distinction between human and machine generated works becomes increasingly blurred
and thus ascertaining the owner of AI-generated content poses a significant challenge to existing
copyright frameworks. Not only this, this work takes a thorough approach towards the question
of originality and creativity in AI-generated works as it challenges the established criteria for
copyright protection. While copyright laws traditionally require a human element of creativity for
protection, AI-generated content lack this element and thus leading to debates as to the threshold
of originality required for legal recognition. In exploring the perplexing terrain of copyright law in
the age of Artificial intelligence, policy makers, lawmakers and stakeholders, must engage in
interdisciplinary discourse to foster powerful legal frameworks that balance the interests of
creators, consumers and society at large. By Addressing all these legal and ethical challenges
posed by AI-driven innovation, society can foster an environment favorable and conducive to
creativity, innovation and equitable access to knowledge in the digital age.

detail.abstract: The Chinese AI regulatory model has been described as state-driven, where the Chinese government seeks technological supremacy by deploying AI to entrench power through surveillance, control, and cooptation of public and private sectors. It is portrayed as a comprehensive, top-down approach with little room for agency, where autocracy and AI innovation mutually reinforce each other. However, this paper provides a more nuanced picture of China's AI governance. We argue that the Chinese government, at both central and local levels, has adopted a subtle and collaborative approach that integrates state action with private capabilities in dynamic ways that are not necessarily autocratic in nature. We demonstrate this through a framework analyzing the Chinese state's role as investor, regulator, and procurer in relation to private AI companies. First, as an investor, instead of being a controlling shareholder, we find that the Chinese government (or its entities) is a non-controlling shareholder who exerts indirect influence through overlooked mechanisms, while preserving governance powers for corporate boards. Second, as a regulator, contrary to assumptions that regulation is enforced through coercive command-and-control methods, we find that local governments rely on financial support to incentivize AI firms to align with the central government's objectives. Finally, as a procurer, contrary to the notion that autocracy reinforces innovation through unrestricted data sharing, we show that legal and institutional restrictions apply, and AI firms often have incentives to use non-government data. These findings complexify conventional narratives of Chinese AI governance and offer insights into the evolving state-private relationship, with implications for global AI governance debates.

detail.abstract: Despite evidence of severe, culturally specific patterns of abuse and persistent barriers to support, little research has focused on the experiences of South Asian women in Scotland or how they understand and seek help for domestic abuse. Diversifying Justice addressed this gap through arts-based focus groups (n=15) and narrative interviews (n=14), conducted in Urdu and English, using a feminist, participatory methodology designed to prioritise care, reciprocity, and safe sharing of experiences. This briefing focuses on help-seeking and understandings of justice. Participants described highly variable service responses, from empowering interventions to harmful failures shaped by cultural insensitivity or “race anxiety.” Justice was often understood not only as punishment but also as acknowledgement, repair, and freedom from abuse. Religion emerged as a vital source of resilience, while natal kin and friendships offered crucial support. Findings underline the need for culturally competent services, peer-led models, and broader conceptions of justice that centre dignity and lived security.

From a grassroots movement for democratic reforms in 2011, the Syrian uprising has now come to an end with the fall of Bashar al-Assad, marking a major turning point for the Middle East. Over the past decade, Syria has been at the centre of the region's geopolitical rivalries, proxy wars, and ideological fights, and Assad's authoritarian rule has been both a manifestation and an epitome of the wider malaise. It is a profound event with wide-reaching implications across the Middle East, as his ouster, coming after years of civil war, foreign interventions, and wavering international support, is not just the end of an era for Syria; rather, it is the beginning of a new era for the country and the geopolitical environment in the Middle East.

It did not happen as an isolated event. Armed opposition groups, combined with the politicisation of the Syrian state, heralded the decline of the monopoly over power held up until then by the Assad regime. Simultaneously, the geopolitical ambitions of powers like Iran, Russia, and Turkey clashed with each other in Syria, and the country itself was a miniaturised version of the wider 'battle for influence' among regional powers.

detail.title: Labor Adjustment Costs and Investment-to-Cash Flow Sensitivities
detail.abstract: This paper examines how labor adjustment costs (LAC) influence investment-cash flow sensitivities (ICFS) using a large sample of U.S. manufacturing firms. Leveraging two complementary identification strategies, a novel labor skills index (LSI) based on detailed occupational data, and a difference-indifferences design exploiting the staggered adoption of state-level employment protection laws over three decades, I find that higher LAC are associated with significantly lower ICFS. This relationship is strongest among firms more reliant on skilled labor, consistent with the notion that labor-intensive adjustments crowd out internal funds otherwise allocated to investment. Contrary to expectations, this effect is not amplified by financial constraints; instead, it appears predominantly among financially unconstrained firms. These findings challenge the traditional interpretation of ICFS as a proxy for financing frictions and suggest that labor market rigidities play a critical role in shaping firm-level investment behavior.

title: African Natural Gas for Europe: Prospects and Challenges

detail.title: African Natural Gas for Europe: Prospects and Challenges
detail.abstract:
The energy crisis in the European market continues. This process has resulted from a combination of factors: accumulated structural imbalances in global energy markets, the energy policies of individual European Union countries and the EU as a whole, the pandemic, and finally, the Special Military Operation that began in February 2022, which caused a reduction in Russian gas supplies to Europe. The EU was unable—if such a goal was even set—to painlessly replace Russian gas from other sources, among which Africa was expected to play a significant role. In the spring of 2022, European high-level delegations visited African countries almost every week, trying to secure increased gas supplies.

According to the author’s estimates, based on data from exporters, importers, and international organizations, African gas exports to the EU in 2022 amounted to 72 billion cubic meters—about 2 billion cubic meters less than in 2021. At the same time, most African exporters (or rather, the Western operators of LNG plants who control LNG marketing) redirected to the EU part of the volumes previously supplied to Asia. Also, in 2022, a new African country entered the global LNG market—Mozambique. In December, Spain received its first LNG shipment produced by Britain’s BP at the Coral Sul floating LNG plant on Mozambique’s offshore shelf.

Within this study, statistics from African exporters, European importers, and international organizations were analyzed. Based on the analysis of the domestic gas markets of African countries (Algeria, Angola, Egypt, Cameroon, Mozambique, Nigeria, Equatorial Guinea), the reasons for the overall decline in supplies are presented, along with forecasts regarding the dynamics of African gas exports to the European Union in the medium term.

detail.abstract: The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act considerably limited federal deductions for state and local tax (SALT) payments, generally to $10,000 for individual taxpayers. In response, many states enacted passthrough entity tax (PTET) laws to facilitate a workaround to this limitation. PTET laws, in effect, allow passthrough business owners to remit their state individual income taxes via their businesses, where SALT deductions are not subject to any limit. Using this workaround, we estimate that passthrough businesses deducted $67 billion of income taxes in 2024, translating to $14 billion in reduced federal revenue and largely benefiting the very top of the income distribution.

Through the perspective of Taylor Jackson, an investment analyst at the California State Teachers' Retirement System (CalSTRS), students will analyze corporate sustainability data from UCLA’s Open for Good Project (OFG). title: Artificial Intelligence Framework for Prioritizing Carbon Capture, and Storage Projects through Decision Analysis
affiliations: Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Ghana

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence Framework for Prioritizing Carbon Capture, and Storage Projects through Decision Analysis
detail.abstract: The complexity operational uncertainty and financial risk of large-scale carbon capture and storage (CCS) projects make traditional evaluation methods relying on expert judgment inadequate. These traditional approaches frequently fall short in identifying the quantifiable elements that contribute to project success underscoring the necessity of methodical and data-driven frameworks for decision support. In this study a predictive model based on artificial intelligence was created to categorize and explain project success using quantifiable project attributes. With an area under the curve (AUC) of 0. 895 and a mean F1-score of 0. 854 the Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) classifier outperformed the other models in the test. Following hyperparameter optimization this performance outperformed the rival approaches and held steady. The ideal setup included 200 boosting iterations a maximum depth of 7 and a learning rate of 0. 05. While the precision-recall (PR) curve showed an average precision of 0. 91 indicating a strong balance between precision and recall across thresholds the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve showed a strong separation between successful and unsuccessful projects (Figure 1). These results show that project outcomes are not arbitrary but rather can be methodically explained by measurable characteristics. The models output was incorporated into a framework for project ranking decision-support building upon these predictive underpinnings. The entropy weighting method revealed the prevailing influence of project scale and storage capacity by objectively assigning importance to evaluation criteria. With a score of 0. 92 the Bell Creek project was determined to be the best choice using the technique for order preference by similarity to the ideal solution (TOPSIS). The Lost Cabin Gas Plant project came in second with a score of 0. 90. The Bell Creek project was given a priority index of 0. 91 while the Lost Cabin project was given a priority index of 0. 89 as confirmed by the preference ranking method for enrichment evaluation (PROMETHEE). According to a sensitivity analysis changes in criterion weights led to a change in project positions of less than 5% further confirming the stability of these rankings. This resilience highlights the frameworks dependability for real-world use. Overall the findings demonstrate that project success in CCS is not random but rather systematically explicable. In order to guide investment and policy decisions in the sustainable energy transition this work offers a transparent and trustworthy tool that bases ranking and prioritization on a validated AI classifier and strong multi-criteria decision-making techniques.

title: Leveraging Sovereign Capital – A Policy Perspective

detail.title: Leveraging Sovereign Capital – A Policy Perspective
detail.abstract: In the world of international capital flows, analysts and policymakers typically focus on private investments. But increasingly, and especially in the past two decades, key participants in cross-border capital flows have been government owned entities-usually referred to as Sovereign Wealth Funds, or SWFs. Today, these SWFs have assets under management (AUM) exceeding USD 13 trillion, making them possibly the most influential class of investors across the world. SWFs are now seen as critical quasi-state actors shaping the global economy of the 21st century. The discussion around SWFs acquired greater relevance recently with an Executive Order 3 issued by the US administration to establish a Sovereign Wealth Fund for the United States. In the past two decades and especially since the Global Financial Crisis of 2007-09, there has been considerable research on the motivations, mandates and investment behavior of SWFs. This paper attempts to review and consolidate the existing literature on the subject from a range of perspectives and to highlight specific policy considerations for SWFs with a focus on the considerations for the host country and its firms that expect to receive and benefit from investments by SWFs. The paper concludes with some policy recommendations.

title: From Research to Reality - Mitigating Live Quant Trading Fragility

detail.title: From Research to Reality - Mitigating Live Quant Trading Fragility
detail.abstract: Quantitative investment models promise systematic, repeatable alpha. Yet allocators and practitioners alike know the frustration of seeing strategies that perform impressively in backtests, only to collapse in live deployment. This paper explores the root causes of this breakdown, focusing on three domains: data integrity, model fragility, and implementation reality. We argue that sustainable quant investing requires robust research processes designed explicitly for noise, decay, and market regime shifts. We propose a framework allocators can use to distinguish between fragile backtests and resilient research pipelines, and highlight principles for building models with a higher probability of surviving contact with live markets.

detail.title: Transfer of Registered Shares under Turkish Law: Key Legal Issues and Practical Considerations
detail.abstract: This article examines the transfer of registered shares under Turkish law. Such transfers are generally based on a prior share purchase agreement, yet in practice a number of difficulties arise in the process of concluding and executing these agreements. The key issues include: (i) the determination of the applicable law in share purchase agreements involving a foreign element; (ii) the permissibility of representation; (iii) the necessity of approvals from various institutions and authorities; (iv) the legal nature of share purchase agreements; and (v) whether break fees stipulated in these agreements fall within the meaning of Article 380 of the Turkish Commercial Code (TCC). Where the shares to be transferred are registered shares, restrictions on transferability (Vinkulierung) contained in the company's Articles of Association may create additional complications under Turkish law. In particular, the potential invalidity of such restrictions pursuant to Article 28(7) of Law No. 6103 on the Entry into Force and Implementation of the TCC, the possibility for the company to invoke a statutory exemption in this context, and the nature, form, and legal consequences of both the notification of transfer authorization and the corresponding entry in the share register warrant independent consideration. The analysis aims to provide both academic insight and practical guidance for lawyers, scholars, and practitioners dealing with cross-border share transfers involving Turkish joint stock companies.

detail.abstract: In the tort of passing off, decision-makers regularly point out the continuity of doctrinal development and the ‘well settled’ nature of the law. Lord Parker’s speech in AG Spalding & Bros v AW Gamage Ltd (1915) plays a prominent role in this story of unfurling progress. In that case, he famously rejected the idea that passing off protects property in unregistered trading signs per se, in favour of a theory that identifies goodwill as the property right underlying the cause of action. This decision is now widely regarded as the moment at which passing off was definitively placed on its modern theoretical foundations. It is argued here that this narrative of the tort’s development conceals a significant, but largely unacknowledged, change that has taken place since Spalding v Gamage. At the time of Lord Parker’s speech, to the extent that it was considered at all, goodwill was envisaged as a relatively undifferentiated right in a claimant’s business. By contrast, today, the right protected by the law of passing off is generally treated as though it subsists directly in individual trading signs. Ironically, therefore, it is difficult to distinguish from the right in unregistered marks so emphatically rejected by Lord Parker himself. This analysis, which is based on a close reading of judgments handed down since 1915, presents a historical account of conceptual and linguistic developments in the tort over the last century or so. In so doing, it questions orthodox narratives about its form and foundations and raises significant questions about the future of the cause of action

Emerging at the intersection of philosophy, futures studies, design, and cultural epistemologies, the work critiques algorithmic rationality and proposes intuition, resonance, and symbolic depth as vital epistemic tools in a post-AI world.

title: Empowering Adoption: Experimental Evidence on Nutritional Seeds Uptake by Ethiopian Women Farmers
affiliations: Haramaya University, University of Groningen - Department of Economics, Econometrics and Finance, Economie and University of Groningen

detail.title: Empowering Adoption: Experimental Evidence on Nutritional Seeds Uptake by Ethiopian Women Farmers
detail.abstract: Despite its significant nutritional benefits, the adoption of Quality Protein Maize (QPM)-a biofortified maize variety rich in lysine and tryptophan-remains low across sub-Saharan Africa. This paper investigates whether psychosocial constraints hinder adoption among smallholder farmers. We conduct a randomized controlled trial with 1,200 female smallholders in Ethiopia to evaluate the impact of a psychosocial training intervention-targeting self-esteem, goal setting, and social capital-on willingness to pay (WTP) for QPM seeds. We elicit WTP through a Becker-DeGroot-Marschak (BDM) auction with randomly assigned strike prices to simulate varying subsidy levels. We find that the training significantly increases both stated WTP and actual adoption: treated participants bid 5.42% higher and were 6.2% more likely to purchase QPM seeds. We further compare the cost-effectiveness of the training to that of a direct seed subsidy, finding that the psychosocial intervention yields comparable uptake effects equivalent to additional subsidy of 30 Birr per participant. These findings highlight the role of internal psychological barriers in shaping agricultural investment decisions and suggest that non-financial interventions can complement traditional subsidy programs to improve uptake of health-enhancing technologies in low-income settings.

title: The Role of Accounting Information for Public Mass Transit Systems in Addressing Polycrisis Risks
affiliations: University of Virginia - Weldon Cooper Center for Public Service

detail.title: The Role of Accounting Information for Public Mass Transit Systems in Addressing Polycrisis Risks
detail.abstract: In the United States, the U.S. Bureau of Economic analysis reports that state and local governments (subnational) own 80 percent of all reported public sector fixed assets 1. This includes buildings, roads and bridges, water and sewer lines, parks and recreational facilities, mass transit systems and other elements. These governmental fixed assets are crucial in driving the economic flows of the $30 trillion U.S. economy. Mass transit systems, as one element of these fixed assets, are improving regional economic development, addressing climate change, economic competitiveness and overall human wellbeing. Simultaneously, these very economic, social and environmental factors pose risks to the operations and viability of these systems. These systems face a tremendous amount of fiscal stress caused by a number of factors including the post pandemic economy, commuting patterns and other social conditions. The system also faces other risks such as the impact of clime change such as extreme heat and flooding that would impact service provision and possibly impose much higher maintenance costs over time. This paper will be divided into several sections. Section one will be in introductory and background section. Part one of section one will highlight the importance the overall role of government fixed and the current of accounting reporting. The next part of section one will focus on the role of mass transit in the overall fixed asset system and any unique accounting challenges in this sector. Section two will provide a conceptual framework for how we can thing about the overall role of financial and sustainability accounting in the mass transit system. This framework will directly assess how accounting information can be used in vulnerability and resiliency analysis beyond the traditional financial and operational metrics. The goal is to develop a normative conceptual framework with a specific set of criteria from which we can judge and assess the ability of the current accounting statements, in a general sense, to inform decision makers and stakeholders regarding the financial, operational and environmental risks facing mass transit systems. The other point of emphasis will be in the framework and reporting that comes out mass transit systems and whether such information meets the informational needs of the various stakeholders in these systems. Section three will be focused on a case study of the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority as a case study for the conceptual framework developed in section two. The Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority (WMATA) is the case study focus of this study and how is implementing and using accounting practices to address these multiple problems. WMATA is the system that serves as the rail and bus system form the Washington, D.C. metropolitan area and it is the second largest system in the United States. Moody’s and standard and Poor’s; have retained a negative of the credit rating for WMATA. The WMATA is a unique government agency in that it is an interstate/federal compact between The United States government, the Commonwealth of Virginia, the State of Maryland and the Washington District of Columbia government.

title: The Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive: A Law & Economics Evaluation
affiliations: The Hadar Jabotinsky Center for Interdisciplinary Research of Financial Markets, Crises and Technology (HJC) and Institute of Law and Economics, University of Hamburg

detail.title: The Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive: A Law & Economics Evaluation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: nothing to declare
declarations.ethicsApproval: Nothing to declare
declarations.funderStatement: The research was funded by the University of Hamburg (excellence cluster)

detail.abstract: The Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CS3D), adopted by the European Union in June 2024, represents an ambitious regulatory experiment that transforms large corporations into gatekeepers of sustainable supply chains. This paper provides a comprehensive Law & Economics analysis of the CS3D, revealing several overlooked incentive problems that may undermine its effectiveness. We identify environmental harm and human rights violations as "public bads" requiring intervention, but demonstrate that the CS3D's mechanisms may create perverse outcomes. Through transaction cost analysis, we further show how the directive may inefficiently allocate monitoring responsibilities. The analysis further reveals risks of both over-deterrence and under-deterrence arising from the problematic combination of regulatory fines and civil liability. Most concerning, we document multiple unintended consequences: chilling effects that may drive firms from markets, a statistical discrimination problem that could harm the very populations the directive aims to protect, higher prices, potential competition effects, and rent-seeking costs due to circumvention attempts.  Our analysis suggests that without careful calibration, the CS3D may trade one set of market failures for another, potentially harming both economic efficiency and the vulnerable populations it seeks to protect.

title: The Economic, Demographic, and Institutional Foundations of Trade Liberalization in Pakistan: An Econometric and Machine Learning Analysis
affiliations: National Research University – Higher School of Economics (HSE University)

detail.title: The Economic, Demographic, and Institutional Foundations of Trade Liberalization in Pakistan: An Econometric and Machine Learning Analysis
detail.abstract: Developing economies face persistent challenges integrating into global trade, shaped by complex economic, demographic, and institutional interactions. This study investigates these multifaceted determinants of trade openness in Pakistan from 1990-2024, employing a robust mixed-methods approach that integrates advanced econometrics with machine learning. Unit root tests revealed a mix of stationary and non-stationary series, justifying the use of an Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) model. Cointegration was confirmed via Johansen and ARDL Bounds tests, and an Error Correction Model (ECM) captured dynamics. To address endogeneity, Instrumental Variables (IV-2SLS) and Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) estimators were applied, while machine learning models (LASSO, Random Forest, SVR) explored non-linearities. The results confirm long-run cointegration among trade and its determinants. Gross capital formation (GCF) was a consistently positive and significant driver, though its effect is constrained by limited foreign direct investment. Conversely, human capital deficiencies (proxied by services value-added) showed a significant negative impact, reflecting skills mismatches that limit competitiveness. Institutional quality, particularly government effectiveness, also negatively impacted trade, highlighting governance weaknesses as a major non-tariff barrier. Inflation had a positive relationship with trade, suggesting liberalization may exacerbate price pressures. The ECM indicated a rapid, potentially volatile adjustment to equilibrium. Machine learning (SVR performed best) reinforced the dominance of economic factors like GCF and inflation, while demographic and institutional variables showed weaker contributions, likely due to data limitations. Pakistan's trade is constrained by low human capital, weak institutions, and macroeconomic imbalances, validating an integrated theoretical framework. Policies must boost investment through FDI, enhance education and vocational training to leverage labor abundance, and implement governance reforms to reduce transaction costs. Macroeconomic stability requires coordinated fiscal and monetary policy. This study contributes a novel methodological framework combining econometrics and machine learning, offering a replicable model for analyzing trade dynamics in developing economies. Future research should utilize sectoral data, incorporate sustainability metrics and extend the analysis for comparative regional insights.

title:
Sharia and Secular Law: A Framework for Legal Pluralism 
A Proposal for Integrating Faith-Based Justice within Secular Societies
affiliations: Federal University of Agriculture

detail.title:
Sharia and Secular Law: A Framework for Legal Pluralism 
A Proposal for Integrating Faith-Based Justice within Secular Societies
detail.abstract: This proposal presents a framework for integrating a Sharia justice system within an existing secular legal structure. The purpose is to respect religious diversity, safeguard Muslim legal autonomy, and strengthen national unity without undermining constitutional principles. The model emphasizes that Sharia is not intended as a replacement of secular law but as a complementary system applicable exclusively to Muslims in matters of family, inheritance, morality, religious obligations, and community welfare. The proposal outlines a dual judicial structure where Sharia courts operate alongside secular courts, supported by a Muslim registration system, zakat administration, and a Sharia enforcement unit within the police. It also recommends conflict resolution mechanisms, constitutional safeguards, and capacity-building initiatives to ensure efficiency and prevent jurisdictional overlap. To address misconceptions, the proposal clarifies the moral foundation of Sharia, highlighting its focus on justice, prevention of crime, accountability, and community welfare. By incorporating international human rights standards, particularly freedom of religion and legal inclusion, the framework ensures that fundamental rights are protected while allowing Muslims to live according to their religious convictions. Implementation is envisioned in phases, beginning with pilot programs in Muslim-majority regions, followed by gradual nationwide integration. Ultimately, the proposal seeks to create a balanced and inclusive justice system that upholds fairness, reduces interfaith tension, and enhances public trust in governance.

title: AI and National Competitiveness: Legal and Policy Pathways for U.S. Tech Leadership
affiliations: George Washington University - School of Business

detail.title: AI and National Competitiveness: Legal and Policy Pathways for U.S. Tech Leadership
detail.abstract: The world is quickly demonstrating that artificial intelligence is changing the global economic power, military capabilities, and strategic influence. The US has been a global technological leader. Still, it is currently confronted by increasing challenges posed by China and the European Union, which are developing broad AI governance and industrial policies. The paper begins by tracking the recent development of AI policy in the United States since the Trump administration. It examines federal and state-level policies through the lens of computer governance, export controls, and regulatory coordination. It measures the combination of industrial policy, security protection, and incentives to innovate based on comparative policy analysis. It identifies opportunities to enhance U.S. policy on research investment, talent development, and harmonized governance structures. The results show that export restrictions are still primarily focused on tangible items, and there is no regulation of cloud and computer access. Fragmented state policies also weaken strategic coherence across the country. Based on global comparisons and U.S. policy review, the paper suggests specific reforms, such as requiring federal computer licensing, applying export regulations to cloud-based services, developing a model AI regulation regime to be used by states, strengthening research incentives, and investing in the development of the workforce. Harmonized together, these actions would bolster the country's overall innovation potential, seal significant security gaps, and make the United States a global benchmark in AI regulation.

title: Legal Regulation of Generative AI and Copyright: U.S. Experience and Prospects for Kazakhstan
